option3: Death hath set his throne upon Mount Zion, and hath devoured the princes at their banquets
option4: For death is come up into our windows, and is entered into our palaces, to cut off the children from without, and the young men from the streets
correct: For death is come up into our windows, and is entered into our palaces, to cut off the children from without, and the young men from the streets
explanation: Death (Mavet/Mot) is personified as a stealthy, inescapable intruder climbing through open upper-story windows to snatch youths and children. Jeremiah 9:21 (KJV) - "For death is come up into our windows, and is entered into our palaces, to cut off the children from without, and the young men from the streets."

question: What three human boasts are firmly prohibited in Jeremiah 9:23?
option1: Let not the wise man glory in his wisdom, neither let the mighty man glory in his might, let not the rich man glory in his riches
option2: Let not the king glory in his crown, neither the priest in his altar, nor the warrior in his bow
option3: Let not the builder glory in his towers, neither the merchant in his gold, nor the scholar in his books
option4: Let not the righteous glory in his sacrifices, neither the prophet in his visions, nor the scribe in his pen
correct: Let not the wise man glory in his wisdom, neither let the mighty man glory in his might, let not the rich man glory in his riches
explanation: Intellectual pride (wisdom), physical/military pride (might), and material pride (riches) are dismissed as worthless grounds for boasting. Jeremiah 9:23 (KJV) - "Thus saith the LORD, Let not the wise man glory in his wisdom, neither let the mighty man glory in his might, let not the rich man glory in his riches:"

question: What alone constitutes the supreme, legitimate boast of a human being in Jeremiah 9:24?
option1: That he hath kept all the commandments of the law and offered the appointed sacrifices of the covenant
option2: That he understandeth and knoweth me, that I am the LORD which exercise lovingkindness, judgment, and righteousness, in the earth
option3: That he hath delivered the poor from oppression and walked humbly before the God of Jacob
option4: That he hath proclaimed the truth among the Gentiles and built up the walls of Jerusalem
correct: That he understandeth and knoweth me, that I am the LORD which exercise lovingkindness, judgment, and righteousness, in the earth
explanation: True glorying lies exclusively in relational knowledge of Yahweh, embracing His core covenant attributes: lovingkindness (chesed), justice (mishpat), and righteousness (tsedaqah). Jeremiah 9:24 (KJV) - "But let him that glorieth glory in this, that he understandeth and knoweth me, that I am the LORD which exercise lovingkindness, judgment, and righteousness, in the earth: for in these things I delight, saith the LORD."

question: What pagan astrological superstitions are the Israelites commanded not to fear in Jeremiah 10:2?
option1: The rising of the dog star and the eclipses of the moon
option2: The signs of heaven; for the heathen are dismayed at them
option3: The omens of passing birds and the casting of astrological lots
option4: The conjunctions of the wandering planets and the signs of the zodiac
correct: The signs of heaven; for the heathen are dismayed at them
explanation: God commands Israel not to panic over celestial phenomena, comets, or astrological horoscopes that terrify pagan idolaters. Jeremiah 10:2 (KJV) - "Thus saith the LORD, Learn not the way of the heathen, and be not dismayed at the signs of heaven; for the heathen are dismayed at them."

question: How does Jeremiah describe the manufacturing and absolute powerlessness of wooden idols in Jeremiah 10:3-5?
option1: They are shaped like royal cherubim, yet have no breath: they cannot save their makers from the sword
option2: They are carved with curious art, but hear no prayer: their eyes cannot behold the affliction of the poor
option3: They are upright as the palm tree, but speak not: they must needs be borne, because they cannot go. Be not afraid of them; for they cannot do evil, neither also is it in them to do good
option4: They stand upon pedestals of marble, yet are broken by a stone: their hands cannot hold a sceptre
correct: They are upright as the palm tree, but speak not: they must needs be borne, because they cannot go. Be not afraid of them; for they cannot do evil, neither also is it in them to do good
explanation: Idols are compared to scarecrows in a cucumber patch ('upright as the palm tree'): inanimate, immobile carved logs needing to be carried, incapable of either harm or blessing. Jeremiah 10:5 (KJV) - "They are upright as the palm tree, but speak not: they must needs be borne, because they cannot go. Be not afraid of them; for they cannot do evil, neither also is it in them to do good."

question: What universal title of sovereign majesty is ascribed to Yahweh in Jeremiah 10:7?
option1: Lord of the Sabaoth
option2: Judge of all the earth
option3: King of eternity
option4: King of nations
correct: King of nations
explanation: Yahweh is uniquely extolled not merely as Israel's territorial God, but as the cosmic 'King of nations' (Melekh ha-goyim) to whom universal reverence belongs. Jeremiah 10:7 (KJV) - "Who would not fear thee, O King of nations? for to thee doth it appertain: forasmuch as among all the wise men of the nations, and in all their kingdoms, there is none like unto thee."

question: From which two distant locations were imported silver plates and refined gold brought to adorn pagan idols in Jeremiah 10:9?
option1: Silver from Tarshish and gold from Uphaz
option2: Silver from Egypt and gold from Ophir
option3: Silver from Sheba and gold from Havilah
option4: Silver from Tyre and gold from Cush
correct: Silver from Tarshish and gold from Uphaz
explanation: Silver hammered into plates came from Tarshish (Spain) and fine gold from Uphaz, dressed in royal blue and purple textiles made by human artisans. Jeremiah 10:9 (KJV) - "Silver spread into plates is brought from Tarshish, and gold from Uphaz, the work of the workman, and of the hands of the founder: blue and purple is their clothing: they are all the work of cunning men."

question: What is unique about the language of Jeremiah 10:11 within the entire Book of Jeremiah?
option1: It is composed in archaic poetic Hebrew derived from the Song of Deborah
option2: It is written in Aramaic as a public declaration to the pagan nations that their false gods will perish
option3: It is inscribed in the royal court dialect of Babylon
option4: It is recorded in the ancient Phoenician script of maritime merchants
correct: It is written in Aramaic as a public declaration to the pagan nations that their false gods will perish
explanation: Jeremiah 10:11 is the solitary verse in the book written in imperial Aramaic, empowering exiled Jews to boldly proclaim to their captors that gods who did not create the universe will perish. Jeremiah 10:11 (KJV) - "Thus shall ye say unto them, The gods that have not made the heavens and the earth, even they shall perish from the earth, and from under these heavens."

question: How does Jeremiah 10:12 summarize God's cosmic triadic work in creating the universe?
option1: He formed the earth by his word, he illuminated the heavens by his light, and he filled the seas by his decree
option2: He founded the mountains by his strength, he guided the stars by his counsel, and he established the deep by his understanding
option3: He hath made the earth by his power, he hath established the world by his wisdom, and hath stretched out the heavens by his discretion
option4: He measured the dust by his hand, he weighed the hills in a balance, and he spread the sky like a tent
correct: He hath made the earth by his power, he hath established the world by his wisdom, and hath stretched out the heavens by his discretion
explanation: Creation reveals three divine attributes: omnipotent power (in making the earth), supreme wisdom (in establishing the world's order), and infinite discretion/understanding (in outstretching the heavens). Jeremiah 10:12 (KJV) - "He hath made the earth by his power, he hath established the world by his wisdom, and hath stretched out the heavens by his discretion."

question: What distinctive title contrasts the true God of Israel with hollow pagan idols in Jeremiah 10:16?
option1: The Shield of Abraham
option2: The Fear of Isaac
option3: The Shepherd of Israel
option4: The portion of Jacob
correct: The portion of Jacob
explanation: Unlike manufactured idols that perish, Yahweh is 'The portion of Jacob' (Cheleq Ya'aqov), the personal Creator who adopts Israel as His inheritance rod. Jeremiah 10:16 (KJV) - "The portion of Jacob is not like them: for he is the former of all things; and Israel is the rod of his inheritance: The LORD of hosts is his name."

question: What dramatic ballistic metaphor does God use to describe the sudden expulsion of Judah's inhabitants into exile in Jeremiah 10:18?
option1: Behold, I will sling out the inhabitants of the land at this once, and will distress them
option2: I will blow them away as dry chaff before the whirlwind
option3: I will cast them as a net into the depths of the sea
option4: I will shatter them like a potter's clay vessel against the wall
correct: Behold, I will sling out the inhabitants of the land at this once, and will distress them
explanation: God compares deportation to a slinger hurling a smooth projectile out of a leather sling pouch: violent, sudden, and distant. Jeremiah 10:18 (KJV) - "For thus saith the LORD, Behold, I will sling out the inhabitants of the land at this once, and will distress them, that they may find it so."

question: What profound philosophical and spiritual confession about human autonomy does Jeremiah voice in Jeremiah 10:23?
option1: The heart of man is deceitful above all things, and desperately wicked: who can know it?
option2: O LORD, I know that the way of man is not in himself: it is not in man that walketh to direct his steps
option3: A man's heart deviseth his way: but the LORD directeth his steps in righteousness
option4: There is a way which seemeth right unto a man, but the end thereof are the ways of death
correct: O LORD, I know that the way of man is not in himself: it is not in man that walketh to direct his steps
explanation: Jeremiah acknowledges humanity's complete inability to independently chart a righteous moral destiny without divine guidance. Jeremiah 10:23 (KJV) - "O LORD, I know that the way of man is not in himself: it is not in man that walketh to direct his steps."

question: What measured plea for discipline does Jeremiah offer in Jeremiah 10:24?
option1: Smite me with thy rod, O God, but spare thy remnant from the sword of the Chaldeans
option2: Purge my iniquity with hyssop, but quench the consuming fire of thy fury
option3: O LORD, correct me, but with judgment; not in thine anger, lest thou bring me to nothing
option4: Hide not thy face from my tears, but remember the covenant of David thy servant
correct: O LORD, correct me, but with judgment; not in thine anger, lest thou bring me to nothing
explanation: The prophet submits to corrective divine discipline, but pleads that it be tempered with judicial equity (mishpat) rather than unmitigated wrath, which would annihilate the nation. Jeremiah 10:24 (KJV) - "O LORD, correct me, but with judgment; not in thine anger, lest thou bring me to nothing."

question: What solemn curse from Deuteronomy 27:26 is reiterated at the beginning of the covenant proclamation in Jeremiah 11:3?
option1: Cursed be he that confirmeth not all the words of this law to do them
option2: Cursed be the nation that forsaketh the commandments of the Lord our God
option3: Cursed be the man that obeyeth not the words of this covenant
option4: Cursed be every one that hangeth on a tree or committeth abomination
correct: Cursed be the man that obeyeth not the words of this covenant
explanation: Jeremiah reinforces the covenant lawsuit by echoing the Deuteronomic curse against covenant breakers. Jeremiah 11:3 (KJV) - "And say thou unto them, Thus saith the LORD God of Israel; Cursed be the man that obeyeth not the words of this covenant,"

question: What graphic metaphor depicts the intense suffering and slavery of Israel in Egypt in Jeremiah 11:4?
option1: The house of bondage
option2: The sea of affliction
option3: The yoke of mud and straw
option4: The iron furnace
correct: The iron furnace
explanation: Egyptian bondage is compared to an 'iron furnace' (kur habarzel), an ancient smelting kiln designed to melt refractory iron ore, depicting extreme crucible suffering. Jeremiah 11:4 (KJV) - "Which I commanded your fathers in the day that I brought them forth out of the land of Egypt, from the iron furnace, saying, Obey my voice, and do them ... so shall ye be my people, and I will be your God:"

question: What shocking political and spiritual discovery did the LORD unveil to Jeremiah in Jeremiah 11:9?
option1: A conspiracy is found among the men of Judah, and among the inhabitants of Jerusalem
option2: A secret covenant with Pharaoh has been sealed by the princes of the palace
option3: An underground sanctuary to Molech hath been uncovered beneath the temple
option4: A band of robbers hath murdered the righteous priests in the gate of Benjamin
correct: A conspiracy is found among the men of Judah, and among the inhabitants of Jerusalem
explanation: A treasonous, systematic rebellion ('conspiracy' / qesher) against Yahweh's covenant had been formed by both civil and religious leaders in Jerusalem. Jeremiah 11:9 (KJV) - "And the LORD said unto me, A conspiracy is found among the men of Judah, and among the inhabitants of Jerusalem."

question: According to what municipal standard did Jerusalem construct altars to Baal in Jeremiah 11:13?
option1: According to the number of the gates of the city walls
option2: According to the number of the streets of Jerusalem have ye set up altars to that shameful thing
option3: According to the families of the high priests of the temple
option4: According to the four corners of the royal palace
correct: According to the number of the streets of Jerusalem have ye set up altars to that shameful thing
explanation: Pagan altars to 'that shameful thing' (bosheth, a polemical replacement for Baal) lined every single street and alley throughout Jerusalem. Jeremiah 11:13 (KJV) - "For according to the number of thy cities were thy gods, O Judah; and according to the number of the streets of Jerusalem have ye set up altars to that shameful thing, even altars to burn incense unto Baal."

question: What botanical title of lush beauty did God once bestow upon Judah, which is now ignited with destructive fire in Jeremiah 11:16?
option1: A royal cedar of Lebanon, tall and excellent
option2: A noble vine of Sorek bearing sweet purple clusters
option3: A green olive tree, fair, and of goodly fruit
option4: A fragrant rose of Sharon flourishing in the valleys
correct: A green olive tree, fair, and of goodly fruit
explanation: Judah was planted as a thriving, fruitful green olive tree; but because of her apostasy, God kindled a roaring tumult of fire to fracture its limbs (Paul later alludes to this in Romans 11). Jeremiah 11:16 (KJV) - "The LORD called thy name, A green olive tree, fair, and of goodly fruit: with the noise of a great tumult he hath kindled fire upon it, and the branches of it are broken."

question: What defenseless creature does Jeremiah compare himself to when unaware of the assassination plot against him in Jeremiah 11:19?
option1: A bird caught in the fowler's snare
option2: A wild roe hunted upon the mountains
option3: A helpless dove driven before the falcon
option4: A lamb or an ox that is brought to the slaughter
correct: A lamb or an ox that is brought to the slaughter
explanation: Echoing Isaiah 53:7, Jeremiah describes his innocent, unsuspecting vulnerability as a trusting sacrificial lamb led unawares to slaughter. Jeremiah 11:19 (KJV) - "But I was like a lamb or an ox that is brought to the slaughter; and I knew not that they had devised devices against me, saying, Let us destroy the tree with the fruit thereof, and let us cut him off from the land of the living, that his name may be no more remembered."

question: What arboricultural metaphor did the conspirators use to describe their assassination plot against Jeremiah in Jeremiah 11:19?
option1: Let us destroy the tree with the fruit thereof, and let us cut him off from the land of the living
option2: Let us burn the branches with fire and uproot the vineyard from our hills
option3: Let us hew down the cedar and cast its trunk into the valley of Hinnom
option4: Let us strip off the leaves and poison the roots that it bud no more
correct: Let us destroy the tree with the fruit thereof, and let us cut him off from the land of the living
explanation: The plotters sought to completely eradicate Jeremiah ('the tree') along with his prophetic messages ('the fruit thereof') from the memory of the living. Jeremiah 11:19 (KJV) - " ... saying, Let us destroy the tree with the fruit thereof, and let us cut him off from the land of the living, that his name may be no more remembered."

question: Who were the conspirators plotting Jeremiah's death, and what ultimatum did they deliver to him in Jeremiah 11:21?
option1: The princes of Zedekiah: 'Surrender to the king of Babylon or thou shalt be cast into the dungeon'
option2: The men of Anathoth: 'Prophesy not in the name of the LORD, that thou die not by our hand'
option3: The false prophets of Hananiah: 'Speak peace unto Zion or thy tongue shall be silenced in the stocks'
option4: The priests of Pashur: 'Cease from blaspheming the temple of Solomon or thou shalt be stoned'
correct: The men of Anathoth: 'Prophesy not in the name of the LORD, that thou die not by our hand'
explanation: The plot originated in Jeremiah's own hometown among his fellow priests of Anathoth, who threatened him with murder if he continued prophesying. Jeremiah 11:21 (KJV) - "Therefore thus saith the LORD of the men of Anathoth, that seek thy life, saying, Prophesy not in the name of the LORD, that thou die not by our hand:"

question: What divine retribution was pronounced against the traitorous men of Anathoth in Jeremiah 11:22-23?
option1: Their houses shall be burned with fire and their cattle carried into Damascus
option2: They shall be sold as slaves unto the Ishmaelites and their fields confiscated
option3: The young men shall die by the sword; their sons and their daughters shall die by famine: and there shall be no remnant of them
option4: They shall be struck with blindness and wander as beggars in the desert
correct: The young men shall die by the sword; their sons and their daughters shall die by famine: and there shall be no remnant of them
explanation: God pronounced complete extinction upon the murderous conspirators of Anathoth: young warriors slain by sword, families starved by siege, leaving no remnant. Jeremiah 11:22-23 (KJV) - "Therefore thus saith the LORD of hosts, Behold, I will punish them: the young men shall die by the sword; their sons and their daughters shall die by famine: And there shall be no remnant of them: for I will bring evil upon the men of Anathoth, even the year of their visitation."

question: How does Jeremiah address God when committing his legal cause into divine hands in Jeremiah 11:20?
option1: O Holy One of Israel, that dwellest between the cherubim
option2: O Almighty God, that hast established the heavens and the earth
option3: O King of nations, whose throne is from everlasting to everlasting
option4: O LORD of hosts, that judgest righteously, that triest the reins and the heart
correct: O LORD of hosts, that judgest righteously, that triest the reins and the heart
explanation: Jeremiah submits his grievance to Yahweh Sabaoth, who penetrates humanity's deepest inner motives - the kidneys ('reins' / kelayot, seat of emotions) and the heart (seat of intellect and will). Jeremiah 11:20 (KJV) - "But, O LORD of hosts, that judgest righteously, that triest the reins and the heart, let me see thy vengeance on them: for unto thee have I revealed my cause."

question: What classic theodicy question does Jeremiah wrestle with at the beginning of Chapter 12?
option1: Why do the heathen rage, and the people imagine a vain thing against the anointed?
option2: How long shall the ungodly triumph, and the workers of iniquity utter hard speeches?
option3: Lord, how are they increased that trouble me! many are they that rise up against me
option4: Wherefore doth the way of the wicked prosper? wherefore are all they happy that deal very treacherously?
correct: Wherefore doth the way of the wicked prosper? wherefore are all they happy that deal very treacherously?
explanation: Jeremiah poses the timeless perplexity of theodicy: why do corrupt, treacherous traitors flourish and live in tranquil prosperity while the faithful suffer? Jeremiah 12:1 (KJV) - "Righteous art thou, O LORD, when I plead with thee: yet let me talk with thee of thy judgments: Wherefore doth the way of the wicked prosper? wherefore are all they happy that deal very treacherously?"

question: What acute contrast describes the superficial religious hypocrisy of the wicked in Jeremiah 12:2?
option1: Thou art near in their mouth, and far from their reins
option2: They honor thee with their lips, but their heart is far from thee
option3: They wear phylacteries upon their brow, but their hands are full of blood
option4: They fast in the public squares, but devour widows' houses in secret
correct: Thou art near in their mouth, and far from their reins
explanation: The wicked freely invoke God's holy name with pious lip-service, while remaining utterly alienated from Him in their inner conscience and emotions ('reins'). Jeremiah 12:2 (KJV) - "Thou hast planted them, yea, they have taken root: they grow, yea, they bring forth fruit: thou art near in their mouth, and far from their reins."

question: What famous running and endurance proverb does God use to challenge Jeremiah to prepare for far greater hardships in Jeremiah 12:5?
option1: If a small fire hath consumed thy vineyard, how wilt thou stand before the furnace of Babylon?
option2: If thou hast run with the footmen, and they have wearied thee, then how canst thou contend with horses? and if in the land of peace, wherein thou trustedst, they wearied thee, then how wilt thou do in the swelling of Jordan?
option3: If the thorns of the desert have pierced thy feet, how wilt thou climb the rocky mountains of judgment?
option4: If the whispering of thy neighbours hath troubled thee, how wilt thou endure the shouting of armed legions?
correct: If thou hast run with the footmen, and they have wearied thee, then how canst thou contend with horses? and if in the land of peace, wherein thou trustedst, they wearied thee, then how wilt thou do in the swelling of Jordan?
explanation: God rebukes Jeremiah's despondency over hometown opposition (footmen) by asking how he will survive royal persecution (cavalry horses), or navigate the lion-infested thickets of the flooded Jordan ('swelling of Jordan' / ge'on hayarden). Jeremiah 12:5 (KJV) - "If thou hast run with the footmen, and they have wearied thee, then how canst thou contend with horses? and if in the land of peace, wherein thou trustedst, they wearied thee, then how wilt thou do in the swelling of Jordan?"

question: What painful domestic betrayal is disclosed to Jeremiah in Jeremiah 12:6?
option1: Thy father hath disinherited thee from the priestly portion of Anathoth
option2: Thy kinsmen have delivered thy mother into the hands of the Chaldeans
option3: Even thy brethren, and the house of thy father, even they have dealt treacherously with thee; yea, they have called a multitude after thee
option4: Thy brothers have sold thy inheritance to the priests of Baal
correct: Even thy brethren, and the house of thy father, even they have dealt treacherously with thee; yea, they have called a multitude after thee
explanation: Jeremiah's own blood brothers and immediate family members betrayed him, organizing an angry mob to hunt him down despite their hypocritical smooth words. Jeremiah 12:6 (KJV) - "For even thy brethren, and the house of thy father, even they have dealt treacherously with thee; yea, they have called a multitude after thee: believe them not, though they speak fair words unto thee."

question: How does God tenderly yet sorrowfully designate the nation He is forced to surrender to her enemies in Jeremiah 12:7?
option1: The daughter of Zion
option2: The apple of mine eye
option3: The vineyard of my delight
option4: The dearly beloved of my soul
correct: The dearly beloved of my soul
explanation: Even as Yahweh delivers Judah to imperial conquerors, He reveals His heartbroken affection, calling her 'the dearly beloved of my soul' (yedidut nafshi). Jeremiah 12:7 (KJV) - "I have forsaken mine house, I have left mine heritage; I have given the dearly beloved of my soul into the hand of her enemies."

question: What aggressive predator does God's heritage become toward Him in Jeremiah 12:8?
option1: Mine heritage is unto me as a lion in the forest; it crieth out against me: therefore have I hated it
option2: A wild wolf prowling in the night, seeking to devour my lambs
option3: A rebellious heifer kicking against the pricks of my law
option4: A poisonous serpent striking at the heel of my messenger
correct: Mine heritage is unto me as a lion in the forest; it crieth out against me: therefore have I hated it
explanation: Instead of submitting as gentle sheep, the covenant people roared against God like a savage, rebellious forest lion. Jeremiah 12:8 (KJV) - "Mine heritage is unto me as a lion in the forest; it crieth out against me: therefore have I hated it."

question: What avian metaphor depicts Judah as an exotic target attacked by encircling birds of prey in Jeremiah 12:9?
option1: A wounded dove trapped in the crags of the rocks
option2: Mine heritage is unto me as a speckled bird, the birds round about are against her
option3: A solitary sparrow sitting upon the housetop
option4: An eagle stripped of her plumage in the wilderness
correct: Mine heritage is unto me as a speckled bird, the birds round about are against her
explanation: Judah is likened to a strangely colored bird ('speckled bird' / 'ayit tsavua') whose odd plumage attracts all the surrounding birds of prey to attack and peck her to death. Jeremiah 12:9 (KJV) - "Mine heritage is unto me as a speckled bird, the birds round about are against her; come ye, assemble all the beasts of the field, come to devour."

question: What devastating impact have corrupt political and religious leaders ('many pastors') inflicted on God's vineyard in Jeremiah 12:10?
option1: They have plucked the ripe grapes, broken down the stone walls, and sold the harvest for silver
option2: They have planted strange briers, neglected the winepress, and burned the watchman's tower
option3: They have destroyed my vineyard, they have trodden my portion under foot, they have made my pleasant portion a desolate wilderness
option4: They have driven away the laborers, withheld the rain, and profaned the holy terraces
correct: They have destroyed my vineyard, they have trodden my portion under foot, they have made my pleasant portion a desolate wilderness
explanation: The nation's rulers ('pastors' / shepherds) trampled God's fertile, cherished heritage into an arid, desolate wasteland. Jeremiah 12:10 (KJV) - "Many pastors have destroyed my vineyard, they have trodden my portion under foot, they have made my pleasant portion a desolate wilderness."

question: What disappointed agricultural outcome illustrates the futility of human labor under divine wrath in Jeremiah 12:13?
option1: They planted choice vines, but reaped wild grapes of bitterness
option2: They sowed sweet barley, but the locusts devoured the green ear
option3: They ploughed fertile valleys, but gathered only thistle and chaff
option4: They have sown wheat, but shall reap thorns: they have put themselves to pain, but shall not profit
correct: They have sown wheat, but shall reap thorns: they have put themselves to pain, but shall not profit
explanation: Judah's agricultural and political toil resulted in bitter frustration: planting wheat but harvesting noxious thorns, laboring in vain. Jeremiah 12:13 (KJV) - "They have sown wheat, but shall reap thorns: they have put themselves to pain, but shall not profit: and they shall be ashamed of your revenues because of the fierce anger of the LORD."

question: What merciful condition will allow Israel's surrounding pagan neighbors (Moab, Ammon, Edom) to be built up in the midst of God's people in Jeremiah 12:16?
option1: If they will diligently learn the ways of my people, to swear by my name, The LORD liveth; as they taught my people to swear by Baal
option2: If they pay tribute of gold and silver annually into the temple of Jerusalem
option3: If they send their princes to be educated in the Torah by the sons of Aaron
option4: If they break down their idols and demolish the high places of Chemosh and Milcom
correct: If they will diligently learn the ways of my people, to swear by my name, The LORD liveth; as they taught my people to swear by Baal
explanation: God extends remarkable missionary grace to Gentile neighbor nations: if they abandon Baal and embrace sincere worship of Yahweh ('The LORD liveth'), they will be incorporated and established as full members of God's people. Jeremiah 12:16 (KJV) - "And it shall come to pass, if they will diligently learn the ways of my people, to swear by my name, The LORD liveth; as they taught my people to swear by Baal; then shall they be built in the midst of my people."

question: What symbolic textile object was Jeremiah commanded to purchase, wear unwashed, and subsequently bury at the Euphrates in Jeremiah 13:1-4?
option1: A linen girdle
option2: A purple mantle
option3: A woollen turban
option4: A scarlet ephod
correct: A linen girdle
explanation: Jeremiah bought a linen waistband ('girdle' / ezor), wore it against his body without washing, and concealed it in a rocky cleft by the Euphrates (Perath). Jeremiah 13:1-4 (KJV) - "Thus saith the LORD unto me, Go and get thee a linen girdle, and put it upon thy loins, and put it not in water ... Take the girdle that thou hast got, which is upon thy loins, and arise, go to Euphrates, and hide it there in a hole of the rock."

question: What condition did the linen girdle exhibit when Jeremiah unearthed it after many days in Jeremiah 13:7?
option1: It was eaten by desert locusts and turned to ash
option2: And, behold, the girdle was marred, it was profitable for nothing
option3: It was bleached pure white by the waters of the river
option4: It was covered with mold and turned into a serpent
correct: And, behold, the girdle was marred, it was profitable for nothing
explanation: Dampness and exposure rotted the buried linen belt until it disintegrated into useless rags, 'profitable for nothing'. Jeremiah 13:7 (KJV) - "Then I went to Euphrates, and digged, and took the girdle from the place where I had hid it: and, behold, the girdle was marred, it was profitable for nothing."

question: What theological meaning did God attribute to the ruined linen girdle in Jeremiah 13:9-11?
option1: As linen is spun from flax, so God wove twelve tribes into a royal garment to conquer the Euphrates
option2: The burial of the girdle represented the seventy years the temple vessels would remain hidden in Babylon
option3: As the girdle cleaveth to the loins of a man, God bound Israel and Judah to Himself to be a praise and glory, but their stubborn idolatry ruined them like the marred girdle
option4: The unwashed belt symbolized the dirty hands of the false prophets who profaned the bronze altar
correct: As the girdle cleaveth to the loins of a man, God bound Israel and Judah to Himself to be a praise and glory, but their stubborn idolatry ruined them like the marred girdle
explanation: Just as an intimate waistcloth clings tightly to a person's body, Yahweh bound Israel to Himself for intimate covenant communion and glory, but apostasy rendered them worthless. Jeremiah 13:11 (KJV) - "For as the girdle cleaveth to the loins of a man, so have I caused to cleave unto me the whole house of Israel and the whole house of Judah, saith the LORD; that they might be unto me for a people, and for a name, and for a praise, and for a glory: but they would not hear."

question: What common drinking proverb did Jeremiah use to deliver a shocking prophecy of divine confusion and self-destruction in Jeremiah 13:12-14?
option1: The cup of the LORD is full of red wine: and the wicked of the earth shall wring out the dregs
option2: A golden cup was Babylon in the LORD's hand, that made all the earth drunken
option3: Let us eat and drink; for tomorrow we shall die by the sword of the Chaldeans
option4: Every bottle shall be filled with wine ... Behold, I will fill all the inhabitants of this land ... with drunkenness. And I will dash them one against another
correct: Every bottle shall be filled with wine ... Behold, I will fill all the inhabitants of this land ... with drunkenness. And I will dash them one against another
explanation: The people cynically replied that every clay wine jar is naturally filled with wine; Jeremiah revealed that God would fill the entire nation with the staggering drunkenness of judgment, smashing them together like clay jugs. Jeremiah 13:12-14 (KJV) - "Therefore thou shalt speak unto them this word; Thus saith the LORD God of Israel, Every bottle shall be filled with wine ... Behold, I will fill all the inhabitants of this land, even the kings that sit upon David's throne, and the priests, and the prophets, and all the inhabitants of Jerusalem, with drunkenness. And I will dash them one against another, even the fathers and the sons together, saith the LORD: I will not pity, nor spare, nor have mercy, but destroy them."

question: What secret pastoral grief will overwhelm Jeremiah if his proud countrymen refuse to hear God's voice in Jeremiah 13:17?
option1: My soul shall weep in secret places for your pride; and mine eye shall weep sore, and run down with tears, because the LORD's flock is carried away captive
option2: I will withdraw into the desert and intercede forty days without food or water
option3: My tongue shall cleave to the roof of my mouth and I will speak no more in the gate
option4: I will rend my garments and pour out dust upon my head before the kings of Judah
correct: My soul shall weep in secret places for your pride; and mine eye shall weep sore, and run down with tears, because the LORD's flock is carried away captive
explanation: Unable to prevent impending tragedy, Jeremiah retreats into solitary concealment to weep bitter, brokenhearted tears over the exile of 'the LORD's flock'. Jeremiah 13:17 (KJV) - "But if ye will not hear it, my soul shall weep in secret places for your pride; and mine eye shall weep sore, and run down with tears, because the LORD's flock is carried away captive."

question: To which royal figures did Jeremiah address the humiliating command to step down from their thrones in Jeremiah 13:18?
option1: Say unto the high priest and the captain of the temple, Strip off your holy garments
option2: Say unto the king and to the queen, Humble yourselves, sit down: for your principalities shall come down, even the crown of your glory
option3: Say unto the princes of Judah and the elders of the gate, Put on sackcloth in the dust
option4: Say unto the governors of the provinces, Lay down your golden sceptres
correct: Say unto the king and to the queen, Humble yourselves, sit down: for your principalities shall come down, even the crown of your glory
explanation: Directed at young King Jehoiachin and the influential Queen Mother Nehushta (later deported in 597 BC), Jeremiah commanded them to vacate royal thrones because their glorious crowns were being stripped away. Jeremiah 13:18 (KJV) - "Say unto the king and to the queen, Humble yourselves, sit down: for your principalities shall come down, even the crown of your glory."

question: What famous anatomical and zoological proverb demonstrates the utter impossibility of habitual sinners reforming themselves in Jeremiah 13:23?
option1: Can an eagle walk like a tortoise, or a raven sing like a nightingale?
option2: Can a wild ass forget her lust, or a desert viper lose her venom?
option3: Can the Ethiopian change his skin, or the leopard his spots? then may ye also do good, that are accustomed to do evil
option4: Can an iron pillar be bent like reeds, or a rock melt like wax in the sun?
correct: Can the Ethiopian change his skin, or the leopard his spots? then may ye also do good, that are accustomed to do evil
explanation: Just as a Cushite cannot alter his skin pigmentation nor a leopard erase its rosette spots, so entrenched habitual sin paralyzes moral self-reformation without sovereign divine regeneration. Jeremiah 13:23 (KJV) - "Can the Ethiopian change his skin, or the leopard his spots? then may ye also do good, that are accustomed to do evil."

question: What agricultural scattering metaphor describes the dispersion of Judah across the nations in Jeremiah 13:24?
option1: As dry chaff blown from the threshing floor into the sea
option2: As withered leaves trampled beneath the feet of wild beasts
option3: As crushed grain discarded outside the camp of the conquerors
option4: As the stubble that passeth away by the wind of the wilderness
correct: As the stubble that passeth away by the wind of the wilderness
explanation: Apostate Judeans will be swept away and scattered like weightless straw stubble driven before the scorching desert wind. Jeremiah 13:24 (KJV) - "Therefore will I scatter them as the stubble that passeth away by the wind of the wilderness."

question: What public humiliation will expose Jerusalem's shameless spiritual adultery in Jeremiah 13:26?
option1: Therefore will I discover thy skirts upon thy face, that thy shame may appear
option2: I will strip off thy royal jewels and cast thy ornaments into the mire
option3: I will shave thy head bald and brand thy forehead with the mark of a harlot
option4: I will lead thee naked through the gates of Babylon before the eyes of all kings
correct: Therefore will I discover thy skirts upon thy face, that thy shame may appear
explanation: Drawing on ancient near eastern punitive customs for convicted adulteresses, God declares He will pull Jerusalem's skirts over her face to publicly expose her disgrace. Jeremiah 13:26 (KJV) - "Therefore will I discover thy skirts upon thy face, that thy shame may appear."

question: With what poignant, yearning plea does Chapter 13 conclude in Jeremiah 13:27?
option1: Turn thou unto me, O daughter of Zion, before the sun goeth down forever
option2: Woe unto thee, O Jerusalem! wilt thou not be made clean? when shall it once be?
option3: How long shall thy vain thoughts lodge within thee, O backsliding people?
option4: Repent and turn from thy idols, lest my wrath burn like an unquenchable fire
correct: Woe unto thee, O Jerusalem! wilt thou not be made clean? when shall it once be?
explanation: Even after cataloging her lewd idolatries upon the hills, God cries out with agonizing paternal longing: 'Wilt thou not be made clean? when shall it once be?' Jeremiah 13:27 (KJV) - "I have seen thine adulteries, and thy neighings, the lewdness of thy whoredom, and thine abominations on the hills in the fields. Woe unto thee, O Jerusalem! wilt thou not be made clean? when shall it once be?"

question: What severe environmental catastrophe provides the setting for the divine lawsuit and lamentation in Jeremiah 14:1-4?
option1: A swarming locust plague that devoured every green herb and stripped the fig trees
option2: A catastrophic drought where the ground is chapt and cisterns contain no water
option3: A devastating earthquake that shook the foundations of the temple and opened deep chasms
option4: A lethal murrain that destroyed all the cattle and horses of the land
correct: A catastrophic drought where the ground is chapt and cisterns contain no water
explanation: A severe prolonged drought ('the dearth' / batstsarot) parched the earth until agricultural soil cracked into fissures ('chapt') and aristocrats' servants returned with empty water jars. Jeremiah 14:1, 4 (KJV) - "The word of the LORD that came to Jeremiah concerning the dearth ... Because the ground is chapt, for there was no rain in the earth, the plowmen were ashamed, they covered their heads."

question: What heartbreaking unnatural behavior in the animal kingdom reflects the catastrophic severity of the drought in Jeremiah 14:5?
option1: The lioness devoured her own whelps in the thickets of Jordan
option2: The wild eagles cast their fledglings from the nest upon the rocks
option3: The hind also calved in the field, and forsook it, because there was no grass
option4: The sheep trampled their lambs at the dry bed of the brook Kidron
correct: The hind also calved in the field, and forsook it, because there was no grass
explanation: Even the naturally devoted mother doe (hind) abandons her newborn fawn in the open field because total lack of green vegetation leaves her unable to lactate. Jeremiah 14:5 (KJV) - "Yea, the hind also calved in the field, and forsook it, because there was no grass."

question: How does Jeremiah describe the desperate plight of wild donkeys during the drought in Jeremiah 14:6?
option1: They galloped toward the Great Sea and plunged into the salt waters
option2: They fell dead along the highway from Dan unto Beersheba
option3: They brayed day and night upon the mountains until their strength vanished
option4: They snuffed up the wind like dragons; their eyes did fail, because there was no grass
correct: They snuffed up the wind like dragons; their eyes did fail, because there was no grass
explanation: Wild asses stood panting on barren ridges, gasping for cooling breezes like jackals ('dragons'), their eyesight failing from systemic dehydration. Jeremiah 14:6 (KJV) - "And the wild asses did stand in the high places, they snuffed up the wind like dragons; their eyes did fail, because there was no grass."

question: What striking metaphors does Jeremiah use in his intercessory prayer to describe God appearing detached from His own land in Jeremiah 14:8-9?
option1: As a stranger in the land, as a wayfaring man that turneth aside to tarry for a night, and as a mighty man that cannot save
option2: As an angry judge refusing to listen, and as a warrior whose sword is sheathed
option3: As a shepherd who hath abandoned his sheep to the wolves of the wilderness
option4: As a king sleeping in his palace while his border cities are burned with fire
correct: As a stranger in the land, as a wayfaring man that turneth aside to tarry for a night, and as a mighty man that cannot save
explanation: Jeremiah boldly pleads with Yahweh, questioning why the Hope of Israel acts like a detached foreigner, an overnight traveler with no stake in the community, or an incapacitated warrior. Jeremiah 14:8-9 (KJV) - "O the hope of Israel, the saviour thereof in time of trouble, why shouldest thou be as a stranger in the land, and as a wayfaring man that turneth aside to tarry for a night? Why shouldest thou be as a man astonied, as a mighty man that cannot save? yet thou, O LORD, art in the midst of us, and we are called by thy name; leave us not."

question: What three instruments of total consumption does God declare He will send against the hypocritical fasts and sacrifices of the people in Jeremiah 14:12?
option1: The fire, the locust, and the drought
option2: The sword, and the famine, and the pestilence
option3: The lion, the leopard, and the wolf
option4: The hail, the earthquake, and the whirlwind
correct: The sword, and the famine, and the pestilence
explanation: This classic prophetic triad - war (sword), siege starvation (famine), and epidemic disease (pestilence) - will devour the unrepentant nation. Jeremiah 14:12 (KJV) - "When they fast, I will not hear their cry; and when they offer burnt offering and an oblation, I will not accept them: but I will consume them by the sword, and by the famine, and by the pestilence."

question: What deceptive message did false prophets proclaim to the citizens of Jerusalem in Jeremiah 14:13?
option1: Pharaoh shall come with ten thousand chariots to break the siege of the king of Babylon
option2: The angels of the LORD shall smite the host of the Chaldeans as in the days of Sennacherib
option3: Ye shall not see the sword, neither shall ye have famine; but I will give you assured peace in this place
option4: The drought shall be turned into rivers of milk and honey before the new moon
correct: Ye shall not see the sword, neither shall ye have famine; but I will give you assured peace in this place
explanation: False prophets seduced the population with delusional assurances of immunity: 'Ye shall not see the sword ... I will give you assured peace'. Jeremiah 14:13 (KJV) - "Then said I, Ah, Lord GOD! behold, the prophets say unto them, Ye shall not see the sword, neither shall ye have famine; but I will give you assured peace in this place."

question: What ironic poetic justice did God pronounce against the false prophets who promised immunity from sword and famine in Jeremiah 14:15?
option1: They shall be stoned to death in the valley of slaughter by their own disciples
option2: Their tongues shall be cut out and cast to the fowls of heaven
option3: They shall be blinded and carried in iron chains to the king of Babylon
option4: By sword and famine shall those prophets be consumed
correct: By sword and famine shall those prophets be consumed
explanation: The very twin judgments the false prophets denied - sword and famine - would specifically hunt down and consume them. Jeremiah 14:15 (KJV) - "Therefore thus saith the LORD concerning the prophets that prophesy in my name, and I sent them not, yet they say, Sword and famine shall not be in this land; By sword and famine shall those prophets be consumed."

question: What grim scene awaits the deceived populace who believed the false prophets in Jeremiah 14:16?
option1: They shall be cast out in the streets of Jerusalem because of the famine and the sword; and they shall have none to bury them
option2: They shall wander into the desert seeking bread and water until they perish
option3: They shall be sold into Egyptian slavery for thirty pieces of silver
option4: They shall be shut up in the fortress of Zion until they devour their own children
correct: They shall be cast out in the streets of Jerusalem because of the famine and the sword; and they shall have none to bury them
explanation: Victims of religious deception share the fate of their deceivers: corpses strewn unburied in Jerusalem's streets, denied funeral rites. Jeremiah 14:16 (KJV) - "And the people to whom they prophesy shall be cast out in the streets of Jerusalem because of the famine and the sword; and they shall have none to bury them, them, their wives, nor their sons, nor their daughters: for I will pour their wickedness upon them."

question: What gruesome contrast does Jeremiah encounter whether he steps out into the open country or enters inside the city walls in Jeremiah 14:18?
option1: In the field: wild beasts devouring the flocks; in the city: thieves plundering the palaces
option2: In the field: the slain with the sword; in the city: them that are sick with famine
option3: In the field: parched crops turning to dust; in the city: fires consuming the gates
option4: In the field: invading cavalry pitching tents; in the city: false prophets casting lots
correct: In the field: the slain with the sword; in the city: them that are sick with famine
explanation: No sanctuary exists anywhere: outside the city walls lurks violent slaughter by enemy swords; inside reigns agonizing slow starvation. Jeremiah 14:18 (KJV) - "If I go forth into the field, then behold the slain with the sword! and if I enter into the city, then behold them that are sick with famine! yea, both the prophet and the priest go about into a land that they know not."

question: What theological argument and cosmic question closes Chapter 14 in Jeremiah 14:22?
option1: Can Baal deliver his worshipers from the heat, or Ashtoreth pour out dew upon the hills?
option2: Who hath measured the waters in the hollow of his hand, and meted out heaven with the span?
option3: Are there any among the vanities of the Gentiles that can cause rain? or can the heavens give showers? art not thou he, O LORD our God?
option4: If the Lord God will not save us, who is he among the gods that can deliver out of his hand?
correct: Are there any among the vanities of the Gentiles that can cause rain? or can the heavens give showers? art not thou he, O LORD our God?
explanation: Jeremiah affirms the absolute sovereignty of Creator God over climate: pagan storm gods (like Baal) are powerless nonentities ('vanities') incapable of producing a single drop of rain. Jeremiah 14:22 (KJV) - "Are there any among the vanities of the Gentiles that can cause rain? or can the heavens give showers? art not thou he, O LORD our God? therefore we will wait upon thee: for thou hast made all these things."

question: Which two supreme intercessors in Israel's history are cited to demonstrate that Judah has crossed the point of no return in Jeremiah 15:1?
option1: Abraham and Elijah
option2: Noah and Job
option3: Moses and Samuel
option4: David and Daniel
correct: Moses and Samuel
explanation: Moses (who interceded after the golden calf, Exodus 32) and Samuel (who interceded against the Philistines, 1 Samuel 7) were Israel's greatest champions of prayer; yet even their combined presence could not avert Judah's judgment. Jeremiah 15:1 (KJV) - "Then said the LORD unto me, Though Moses and Samuel stood before me, yet my mind could not be toward this people: cast them out of my sight, and let them go forth."

question: What grim fourfold destiny awaits the apostate population when they ask 'Whither shall we go forth?' in Jeremiah 15:2?
option1: One fourth to the fire, one fourth to the wilderness, one fourth to the sea, and one fourth to exile
option2: The princes to judgment, the priests to slaughter, the elders to poverty, and the children to slavery
option3: The rebellious to the sword, the cowards to the rocks, the wealthy to tribute, and the poor to dust
option4: Such as are for death, to death; and such as are for the sword, to the sword; and such as are for the famine, to the famine; and such as are for the captivity, to the captivity
correct: Such as are for death, to death; and such as are for the sword, to the sword; and such as are for the famine, to the famine; and such as are for the captivity, to the captivity
explanation: God assigns the doomed populace to four inevitable categories of judgment: pestilence/death, sword, famine, and foreign captivity. Jeremiah 15:2 (KJV) - "And it shall come to pass, if they say unto thee, Whither shall we go forth? then thou shalt tell them, Thus saith the LORD; Such as are for death, to death; and such as are for the sword, to the sword; and such as are for the famine, to the famine; and such as are for the captivity, to the captivity."

question: What four predatory destroyers does God appoint over the doomed corpses of His people in Jeremiah 15:3?
option1: The sword to slay, and the dogs to tear, and the fowls of the heaven, and the beasts of the earth, to devour and destroy
option2: The fire to burn, the worms to consume, the wind to scatter, and the desert to swallow
option3: The jackals to gnaw, the vultures to pick, the lions to crush, and the earth to refuse burial
option4: The Chaldean warriors, the Scythian archers, the Arabian nomads, and the Syrian plunderers
correct: The sword to slay, and the dogs to tear, and the fowls of the heaven, and the beasts of the earth, to devour and destroy
explanation: God appoints four executioners: swords for initial slaughter, followed by street dogs, birds of prey, and wild carnivores to desecrate and scatter the remains. Jeremiah 15:3 (KJV) - "And I will appoint over them four kinds, saith the LORD: the sword to slay, and the dogs to tear, and the fowls of the heaven, and the beasts of the earth, to devour and destroy."

question: Whose notorious historic idolatry and shed innocent blood is singled out as the decisive catalyst for Judah's exile in Jeremiah 15:4?
option1: Ahab the son of Omri king of Israel
option2: Manasseh the son of Hezekiah king of Judah
option3: Ahaz the son of Jotham king of Judah
option4: Jehoiakim the son of Josiah king of Judah
correct: Manasseh the son of Hezekiah king of Judah
explanation: King Manasseh's horrific fifty-five-year reign - introducing child sacrifice and filling Jerusalem with innocent blood - corrupted Judah beyond the threshold of national survival (2 Kings 21:11-16). Jeremiah 15:4 (KJV) - "And I will cause them to be removed into all kingdoms of the earth, because of Manasseh the son of Hezekiah king of Judah, for that which he did in Jerusalem."

question: What striking maternal tragedy depicts the sudden total bereavement of the nation in Jeremiah 15:9?
option1: The barren woman that rejoiced is become a widow weeping in the ash heap
option2: The mother of the royal princes hath rent her veil and died upon the battlefield
option3: She that hath borne seven languisheth: she hath given up the ghost; her sun is gone down while it was yet day
option4: She that nourished tender daughters hath sold them for bread during the siege
correct: She that hath borne seven languisheth: she hath given up the ghost; her sun is gone down while it was yet day
explanation: Bearing seven sons was ancient Israel's pinnacle of maternal blessing; yet here the ideal mother loses all seven sons simultaneously, collapsing in grief as her sun sets at high noon. Jeremiah 15:9 (KJV) - "She that hath borne seven languisheth: she hath given up the ghost; her sun is gone down while it was yet day: she hath been ashamed and confounded: and the residue of them will I deliver to the sword before their enemies, saith the LORD."

question: What personal lamentation to his mother does Jeremiah utter regarding his universal societal rejection in Jeremiah 15:10?
option1: Why didst thou not slay me in the womb, that my mother might have been my grave?
option2: Cursed be the day wherein I was born: let not the day wherein my mother bare me be blessed
option3: Behold, I am become a byword among the priests, and a song of drunkards at the gate
option4: Woe is me, my mother, that thou hast borne me a man of strife and a man of contention to the whole earth! I have neither lent on usury, nor men have lent to me on usury; yet every one of them doth curse me
correct: Woe is me, my mother, that thou hast borne me a man of strife and a man of contention to the whole earth! I have neither lent on usury, nor men have lent to me on usury; yet every one of them doth curse me
explanation: Though innocent of financial exploitation or debt litigation (the most common cause of bitter lawsuits), Jeremiah was universally hated and cursed simply for proclaiming God's truth. Jeremiah 15:10 (KJV) - "Woe is me, my mother, that thou hast borne me a man of strife and a man of contention to the whole earth! I have neither lent on usury, nor men have lent to me on usury; yet every one of them doth curse me."

question: What profound experience of spiritual digestion and delight does Jeremiah describe regarding Scripture in Jeremiah 15:16?
option1: Thy words were found, and I did eat them; and thy word was unto me the joy and rejoicing of mine heart: for I am called by thy name, O LORD God of hosts
option2: Thy word is a lamp unto my feet, and a light unto my path in the day of darkness
option3: More to be desired are thy judgments than gold, yea, than much fine gold: sweeter also than honey
option4: I have esteemed the words of his mouth more than my necessary food day and night
correct: Thy words were found, and I did eat them; and thy word was unto me the joy and rejoicing of mine heart: for I am called by thy name, O LORD God of hosts
explanation: Jeremiah internalized, consumed, and assimilated God's revelation, finding inner joy and sustaining nourishment despite outward hostility. Jeremiah 15:16 (KJV) - "Thy words were found, and I did eat them; and thy word was unto me the joy and rejoicing of mine heart: for I am called by thy name, O LORD God of hosts."

question: What agonizing complaint of divine unreliability does Jeremiah voice in the depths of his depression in Jeremiah 15:18?
option1: My soul is weary of my life; I will leave my complaint upon myself; I will speak in bitterness
option2: Why is my pain perpetual, and my wound incurable, which refuseth to be healed? wilt thou be altogether unto me as a liar, and as waters that fail?
option3: Hath God forgotten to be gracious? hath he in anger shut up his tender mercies forever?
option4: Why standest thou afar off, O LORD? why hidest thou thyself in times of trouble?
correct: Why is my pain perpetual, and my wound incurable, which refuseth to be healed? wilt thou be altogether unto me as a liar, and as waters that fail?
explanation: In extreme anguish, Jeremiah compares God to a deceptive desert wadi ('waters that fail' / akhzav) that dries up in scorching summer heat just when the parched traveler needs water most. Jeremiah 15:18 (KJV) - "Why is my pain perpetual, and my wound incurable, which refuseth to be healed? wilt thou be altogether unto me as a liar, and as waters that fail?"

question: What divine condition does God set before Jeremiah to restore him to prophetic authority in Jeremiah 15:19?
option1: Fast forty days on Mount Horeb and offer a clean sacrifice upon the altar of Elijah
option2: Cleanse thy lips with a burning coal and forgive the men of Anathoth from thy heart
option3: If thou return, then will I bring thee again, and thou shalt stand before me: and if thou take forth the precious from the vile, thou shalt be as my mouth: let them return unto thee; but return not thou unto them
option4: Depart from the city of Jerusalem and prophesy only unto the exiles of Babylon
correct: If thou return, then will I bring thee again, and thou shalt stand before me: and if thou take forth the precious from the vile, thou shalt be as my mouth: let them return unto thee; but return not thou unto them
explanation: God gently rebukes His prophet: Jeremiah must repent of cynical despair, filter pure faith from impure bitter complaints ('take forth the precious from the vile'), and refuse to compromise with the corrupt crowd. Jeremiah 15:19 (KJV) - "Therefore thus saith the LORD, If thou return, then will I bring thee again, and thou shalt stand before me: and if thou take forth the precious from the vile, thou shalt be as my mouth: let them return unto thee; but return not thou unto them."

question: What promise of defensive invincibility does God reaffirm to Jeremiah upon his restoration in Jeremiah 15:20?
option1: I will give thee the shield of David and the sword of Gideon to subdue thy adversaries
option2: No plague shall come nigh thy dwelling, and angels shall bear thee up in their hands
option3: Thy persecutors shall stumble and be greatly ashamed, their everlasting confusion never forgotten
option4: I will make thee unto this people a fenced brasen wall: and they shall fight against thee, but they shall not prevail against thee: for I am with thee to save thee and to deliver thee
correct: I will make thee unto this people a fenced brasen wall: and they shall fight against thee, but they shall not prevail against thee: for I am with thee to save thee and to deliver thee
explanation: Reiterating his foundational inaugural call (Jeremiah 1:18-19), God promises that Jeremiah will stand as an impenetrable bronze wall against societal pressure. Jeremiah 15:20 (KJV) - "And I will make thee unto this people a fenced brasen wall: and they shall fight against thee, but they shall not prevail against thee: for I am with thee to save thee and to deliver thee, saith the LORD."

question: What radical domestic restriction did God impose upon Jeremiah as a living prophetic sign in Jeremiah 16:2?
option1: Thou shalt not build an house of stone, but dwell in a nomadic tent all thy days
option2: Thou shalt not drink wine nor eat any pleasant bread until Jerusalem be taken
option3: Thou shalt not purchase land nor inherit the fields of thy fathers in Anathoth
option4: Thou shalt not take thee a wife, neither shalt thou have sons or daughters in this place
correct: Thou shalt not take thee a wife, neither shalt thou have sons or daughters in this place
explanation: Jeremiah was commanded to remain celibate as an enacted sign of the impending horrific deaths awaiting Judean parents and children in the coming siege. Jeremiah 16:2 (KJV) - "Thou shalt not take thee a wife, neither shalt thou have sons or daughters in this place."

question: What second social prohibition forbade Jeremiah from expressing sympathy during bereavement in Jeremiah 16:5?
option1: Enter not into the house of mourning, neither go to lament nor bemoan them: for I have taken away my peace from this people
option2: Touch not a dead body, nor wash the garments of the deceased
option3: Shave not thy beard, nor rend thy mantle at the grave of thy kinsmen
option4: Pour out no oil upon the burial stones, nor offer funeral bread in the gate
correct: Enter not into the house of mourning, neither go to lament nor bemoan them: for I have taken away my peace from this people
explanation: Jeremiah was forbidden to participate in funeral wakes or mourning customs because God had formally withdrawn His shalom, lovingkindness, and mercy from the nation. Jeremiah 16:5 (KJV) - "For thus saith the LORD, Enter not into the house of mourning, neither go to lament nor bemoan them: for I have taken away my peace from this people, saith the LORD, even lovingkindness and mercies."

question: What third social restriction prevented Jeremiah from participating in community celebrations in Jeremiah 16:8?
option1: Drink no wine at the marriage supper of the princes of Judah
option2: Thou shalt not also go into the house of feasting, to sit with them to eat and to drink
option3: Play upon no instrument of music in the feast of tabernacles
option4: Bring no peace offerings to sit at the festival table of the priests
correct: Thou shalt not also go into the house of feasting, to sit with them to eat and to drink
explanation: Jeremiah was barred from banquet halls, wedding feasts, and social celebrations, embodying total isolation amidst an unheeding populace on the brink of catastrophe. Jeremiah 16:8 (KJV) - "Thou shalt not also go into the house of feasting, to sit with them to eat and to drink."

question: What historical liberation oath will be completely eclipsed by the future return from Babylonian exile in Jeremiah 16:14-15?
option1: The LORD liveth, that divided the Red Sea and destroyed Pharaoh's chariots; but, The LORD liveth, that dried up the Euphrates
option2: The LORD liveth, that gave the law upon fiery Mount Sinai; but, The LORD liveth, that wrote his law in our hearts
option3: It shall no more be said, The LORD liveth, that brought up the children of Israel out of the land of Egypt; but, The LORD liveth, that brought up the children of Israel from the land of the north
option4: The LORD liveth, that fed our fathers with manna in the wilderness; but, The LORD liveth, that restored Zion
correct: It shall no more be said, The LORD liveth, that brought up the children of Israel out of the land of Egypt; but, The LORD liveth, that brought up the children of Israel from the land of the north
explanation: The miraculous repatriation of Jewish exiles from the northern empire of Babylon and all global dispersions will surpass even the foundational Exodus from Egypt as the supreme benchmark of redemption. Jeremiah 16:14-15 (KJV) - "Therefore, behold, the days come, saith the LORD, that it shall no more be said, The LORD liveth, that brought up the children of Israel out of the land of Egypt; But, The LORD liveth, that brought up the children of Israel from the land of the north, and from all the lands whither he had driven them: and I will bring them again into their land that I gave unto their fathers."

question: What two occupational metaphors describe the relentless agents God will commission to round up every fugitive Judean in Jeremiah 16:16?
option1: Shepherds with iron crooks, and watchmen with silver horns
option2: Reapers with sharp sickles, and threshers with heavy cart wheels
option3: Fowlers with deceptive snares, and miners digging into the earth
option4: Fishers to fish them, and hunters to hunt them from every mountain, hill, and hole of the rocks
correct: Fishers to fish them, and hunters to hunt them from every mountain, hill, and hole of the rocks
explanation: Invading armies will act first as commercial fishermen sweeping human nets across the land, and then as relentless hunters tracking down every hidden refugee in rocky caverns. Jeremiah 16:16 (KJV) - "Behold, I will send for many fishers, saith the LORD, and they shall fish them; and after will I send for many hunters, and they shall hunt them from every mountain, and from every hill, and out of the holes of the rocks."

question: Why does God declare He will recompense Judah's iniquity and sin double in Jeremiah 16:18?
option1: Because they have defiled my land, they have filled mine inheritance with the carcases of their detestable and abominable things
option2: Because they broke the Sabbath covenant and oppressed the fatherless and widow
option3: Because they made treaties of blood with Egypt and refused the yoke of Babylon
option4: Because they mocked the prophets and murdered the righteous priests in the temple
correct: Because they have defiled my land, they have filled mine inheritance with the carcases of their detestable and abominable things
explanation: Judah polluted the holy inheritance by stuffing the sacred land with lifeless, decaying idolatrous filth ('carcases of their detestable things'). Jeremiah 16:18 (KJV) - "And first I will recompense their iniquity and their sin double; because they have defiled my land, they have filled mine inheritance with the carcases of their detestable and abominable things."

question: What remarkable eschatological pilgrimage of Gentile nations is prophesied in Jeremiah 16:19?
option1: All kings shall fall down before the Son of David, and bring gifts of gold and frankincense
option2: The Gentiles shall come unto thee from the ends of the earth, and shall say, Surely our fathers have inherited lies, vanity, and things wherein there is no profit
option3: The heathen shall assemble on Mount Zion to learn the Torah and beat their swords into plowshares
option4: The islands of Chittim shall send ships of silver to rebuild the burned palaces of Jerusalem
correct: The Gentiles shall come unto thee from the ends of the earth, and shall say, Surely our fathers have inherited lies, vanity, and things wherein there is no profit
explanation: While Judah clings to worthless idols, pagan Gentile nations from the ends of the earth will experience global awakening, renouncing ancestral paganism as useless lies and turning to Yahweh. Jeremiah 16:19 (KJV) - "O LORD, my strength, and my fortress, and my refuge in the day of affliction, the Gentiles shall come unto thee from the ends of the earth, and shall say, Surely our fathers have inherited lies, vanity, and things wherein there is no profit."

question: What biting rhetorical question exposes the absurdity of human manufacturing of deities in Jeremiah 16:20?
option1: Can an earthen vessel command the hands of the potter that fashioned it?
option2: Can silver and gold give breath to a block of wood carved with an axe?
option3: Shall a man make gods unto himself, and they are no gods?
option4: Will a carved rock arise and deliver a man in the day of battle?
correct: Shall a man make gods unto himself, and they are no gods?
explanation: Jeremiah highlights the metaphysical contradiction: a mortal creature attempting to manufacture his own immortal Creator! Jeremiah 16:20 (KJV) - "Shall a man make gods unto himself, and they are no gods?"

question: What sovereign revelation does God declare He will cause the nations to know 'this once' in Jeremiah 16:21?
option1: They shall know that Zion is the holy mountain of the eternal King
option2: They shall know that my covenant with David can never be disannulled
option3: They shall know that I have judged the prince of Babylon in righteousness
option4: I will cause them to know mine hand and my might; and they shall know that my name is The LORD
correct: I will cause them to know mine hand and my might; and they shall know that my name is The LORD
explanation: Through the devastating judgment and subsequent miraculous restoration of Israel, God will demonstrate His omnipotent power to the global community, proving that His name is Yahweh. Jeremiah 16:21 (KJV) - "Therefore, behold, I will this once cause them to know, I will cause them to know mine hand and my might; and they shall know that my name is The LORD."

question: What three personal titles of protection does Jeremiah ascribe to God in his prayer of faith in Jeremiah 16:19?
option1: My strength, and my fortress, and my refuge in the day of affliction
option2: My rock, my shield, and the horn of my salvation
option3: My shepherd, my light, and my everlasting defense
option4: My king, my judge, and my redeemer from the pit
correct: My strength, and my fortress, and my refuge in the day of affliction
explanation: Jeremiah anchors his troubled soul in three divine attributes: personal strength (oz), an unassailable stronghold (ma'oz), and a secure sanctuary (manos) in times of distress. Jeremiah 16:19 (KJV) - "O LORD, my strength, and my fortress, and my refuge in the day of affliction, the Gentiles shall come unto thee from the ends of the earth ... "

question: What indelible tools and recording media illustrate the permanence of Judah's sin in Jeremiah 17:1?
option1: Written with a pen of iron, and with the point of a diamond: it is graven upon the table of their heart, and upon the horns of your altars
option2: Inscribed with lead on stone tablets, and sealed with the signet of the king of Babylon
option3: Drawn with a reed of brass upon parchment, and stored in the archives of the temple
option4: Branded with hot coals upon their foreheads, and carved upon the cedar pillars of their palaces
correct: Written with a pen of iron, and with the point of a diamond: it is graven upon the table of their heart, and upon the horns of your altars
explanation: Judah's apostasy was permanently etched like an inscription cut into rock using an iron stylus tipped with industrial diamond, engraved onto their inner hearts and the blood-splashed horns of their pagan altars. Jeremiah 17:1 (KJV) - "The sin of Judah is written with a pen of iron, and with the point of a diamond: it is graven upon the table of their heart, and upon the horns of your altars;"

question: What botanical and geographical metaphor describes the cursed fate of the person who relies on human flesh rather than God in Jeremiah 17:5-6?
option1: He shall be like a withered vine in the valley of Hinnom, burned with pitch and brimstone
option2: He shall be like the heath in the desert, and shall not see when good cometh; but shall inhabit the parched places in the wilderness, in a salt land and not inhabited
option3: He shall be like a dry reed in the brook Kidron, trampled down by the feet of beasts
option4: He shall be like a solitary thorn bush on Mount Gilboa, upon which neither rain nor dew falleth
correct: He shall be like the heath in the desert, and shall not see when good cometh; but shall inhabit the parched places in the wilderness, in a salt land and not inhabited
explanation: The humanistic person who trusts in human power is likened to a stunted, shriveled juniper shrub ('heath' / ar'ar) surviving in sterile salt flats, oblivious to seasonal rains. Jeremiah 17:5-6 (KJV) - "Thus saith the LORD; Cursed be the man that trusteth in man, and maketh flesh his arm, and whose heart departeth from the LORD. For he shall be like the heath in the desert, and shall not see when good cometh; but shall inhabit the parched places in the wilderness, in a salt land and not inhabited."

question: How does Jeremiah 17:7-8 describe the resilient prosperity of the person who trusts in the LORD?
option1: As a cedar of Lebanon with roots deep in the rocks, which no stormy wind can shake
option2: As an olive tree in the garden of kings, yielding choice oil thirtyfold and sixtyfold
option3: As a tree planted by the waters ... her leaf shall be green; and shall not be careful in the year of drought, neither shall cease from yielding fruit
option4: As a palm tree in the oasis of Jericho, flourishing under the morning sun and evening dew
correct: As a tree planted by the waters ... her leaf shall be green; and shall not be careful in the year of drought, neither shall cease from yielding fruit
explanation: Echoing Psalm 1, the believer who trusts God sends deep taproots into sub-surface river aquifers, thriving with evergreen foliage and uninterrupted fruitfulness even in blazing droughts. Jeremiah 17:7-8 (KJV) - "Blessed is the man that trusteth in the LORD, and whose hope the LORD is. For he shall be as a tree planted by the waters, and that spreadeth out her roots by the river, and shall not see when heat cometh, but her leaf shall be green; and shall not be careful in the year of drought, neither shall cease from yielding fruit."

question: What classic diagnosis of the universal fallen human condition is revealed in Jeremiah 17:9?
option1: The imagination of man's heart is evil from his youth continually: who can change it?
option2: Out of the heart proceed evil thoughts, murders, adulteries, and blasphemies: who can cleanse it?
option3: The heart of the sons of men is full of evil, and madness is in their heart while they live
option4: The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately wicked: who can know it?
correct: The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately wicked: who can know it?
explanation: Scripture exposes the incurable treachery and self-deceit of fallen human nature: 'deceitful above all things, and desperately wicked' ('aqov mikol ve'anush hu). Jeremiah 17:9 (KJV) - "The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately wicked: who can know it?"

question: Who alone possesses the diagnostic capacity to penetrate and evaluate the human heart in Jeremiah 17:10?
option1: I the LORD search the heart, I try the reins, even to give every man according to his ways, and according to the fruit of his doings
option2: The Spirit of God that searcheth all things, yea, the deep things of wisdom
option3: The word of God which is quick, and powerful, and sharper than any twoedged sword
option4: The wisdom of the Almighty which weigheth the spirits of all flesh in righteous scales
correct: I the LORD search the heart, I try the reins, even to give every man according to his ways, and according to the fruit of his doings
explanation: Yahweh alone has sovereign insight to fathom the hidden subconscious depths of the human heart and innermost thoughts ('reins'). Jeremiah 17:10 (KJV) - "I the LORD search the heart, I try the reins, even to give every man according to his ways, and according to the fruit of his doings."

question: What ornithological proverb exposes the tragedy of unjust wealth accumulation in Jeremiah 17:11?
option1: As the ostrich leaveth her eggs in the dust, forgetting that the foot may crush them; so is the miser
option2: As the partridge sitteth on eggs, and hatcheth them not; so he that getteth riches, and not by right, shall leave them in the midst of his days, and at his end shall be a fool
option3: As the eagle buildeth her nest on high, yet her young are taken by the hunter; so are ill-gotten treasures
option4: As the raven gathereth food for her brood, but the whirlwind scattereth it; so shall the extortioner perish
correct: As the partridge sitteth on eggs, and hatcheth them not; so he that getteth riches, and not by right, shall leave them in the midst of his days, and at his end shall be a fool
explanation: Based on ancient folklore where a partridge incubates eggs she did not lay only for the hatchlings to desert her, ill-gotten wealth abruptly abandons the thief in prime of life, leaving him a certified fool (naval). Jeremiah 17:11 (KJV) - "As the partridge sitteth on eggs, and hatcheth them not; so he that getteth riches, and not by right, shall leave them in the midst of his days, and at his end shall be a fool."

question: What fate awaits those who abandon Yahweh, the fountain of living waters, in Jeremiah 17:13?
option1: They shall be blotted out of the book of the living and their memory extinguished
option2: They shall wander as dry dust before the whirlwind into the abyss
option3: They that depart from me shall be written in the earth, because they have forsaken the LORD, the fountain of living waters
option4: Their names shall be carved upon the crumbling rocks of the desert
correct: They that depart from me shall be written in the earth, because they have forsaken the LORD, the fountain of living waters
explanation: While the names of the righteous are inscribed in the permanent book of life, apostates are 'written in the earth' (dust), their fleeting identities erased by passing winds. Jeremiah 17:13 (KJV) - "O LORD, the hope of Israel, all that forsake thee shall be ashamed, and they that depart from me shall be written in the earth, because they have forsaken the LORD, the fountain of living waters."

question: What reciprocal prayer for physical and spiritual restoration does Jeremiah pray in Jeremiah 17:14?
option1: Cleanse me, O LORD, and I shall be clean; wash me, and I shall be whiter than snow
option2: Turn thou me, O LORD, and I shall be turned; restore my soul, for thy mercy endureth forever
option3: Deliver me from my persecutors, O LORD, and I shall be safe; shelter me under thy wings
option4: Heal me, O LORD, and I shall be healed; save me, and I shall be saved: for thou art my praise
correct: Heal me, O LORD, and I shall be healed; save me, and I shall be saved: for thou art my praise
explanation: Jeremiah seeks ultimate healing and salvation exclusively from Yahweh, recognizing that divine deliverance is permanent and complete. Jeremiah 17:14 (KJV) - "Heal me, O LORD, and I shall be healed; save me, and I shall be saved: for thou art my praise."

question: What specific covenant violation at the city gates is highlighted as a primary test of national obedience in Jeremiah 17:21-22?
option1: Bearing burdens and conducting commercial trade on the Sabbath day
option2: Levying unjust taxes on the poor and taking bribes at the city gate
option3: Erecting pagan idols of Baal and Ashtoreth at the entrance of Jerusalem
option4: Refusing to open the gates to the Levites and prophets of the Lord
correct: Bearing burdens and conducting commercial trade on the Sabbath day
explanation: Desecrating the Sabbath by transporting commercial merchandise through Jerusalem's gates became a primary symptom of Judah's secularized rebellion.
