Jeremiah 17:21-22 (KJV) - "Thus saith the LORD; Take heed to yourselves, and bear no burden on the sabbath day, nor bring it in by the gates of Jerusalem; Neither carry forth a burden out of your houses on the sabbath day, neither do ye any work, but hallow ye the sabbath day, as I commanded your fathers."

question: What alternate outcomes does God set before Jerusalem depending on their response to the Sabbath in Jeremiah 17:24-27?
option1: If they obey: rains of blessing and bumper crops; if not: seven years of famine and locusts
option2: If they hallow the Sabbath: Davidic kings and princes shall enter Jerusalem's gates forever; if not: God will kindle an unquenchable fire in the gates to devour the palaces
option3: If they obey: victory over the king of Babylon; if not: immediate slaughter by the sword
option4: If they obey: gold of Ophir flowing into the temple; if not: the Ark of the Covenant carried into exile
correct: If they hallow the Sabbath: Davidic kings and princes shall enter Jerusalem's gates forever; if not: God will kindle an unquenchable fire in the gates to devour the palaces
explanation: Faithful Sabbath sanctification would preserve the Davidic dynasty and Jerusalem's palaces permanently; continuing Sabbath violation would result in unquenchable fire consuming the royal city. Jeremiah 17:25, 27 (KJV) - "Then shall there enter into the gates of this city kings and princes sitting upon the throne of David ... and this city shall remain for ever ... But if ye will not hearken unto me to hallow the sabbath day ... then will I kindle a fire in the gates thereof, and it shall devour the palaces of Jerusalem, and it shall not be quenched."

question: To whose workshop was Jeremiah instructed to go down to receive a vivid visual revelation of divine sovereignty in Jeremiah 18:2?
option1: The silversmith's forge
option2: The potter's house
option3: The fuller's field
option4: The tanner's lodge
correct: The potter's house
explanation: Jeremiah was directed to the potter's workshop in the lower Hinnom Valley, where clay was shaped on horizontal spinning wheels. Jeremiah 18:2-3 (KJV) - "Arise, and go down to the potter's house, and there I will cause thee to hear my words. Then I went down to the potter's house, and, behold, he wrought a work on the wheels."

question: What happened to the clay vessel on the wheel, and how did the potter respond in Jeremiah 18:4?
option1: The clay cracked and flew off the wheel, so the potter swept the fragments into the dust
option2: The vessel dried too quickly in the wind, so the potter threw it into the burning kiln
option3: The vessel that he made of clay was marred in the hand of the potter: so he made it again another vessel, as seemed good to the potter to make it
option4: The wheel broke beneath the weight of the clay, so the potter ceased from his labor
correct: The vessel that he made of clay was marred in the hand of the potter: so he made it again another vessel, as seemed good to the potter to make it
explanation: When an imperfection in the clay deformed the spinning pot, the craftsman crushed it back into a lump and reshaped it into a different vessel according to his sovereign discretion. Jeremiah 18:4 (KJV) - "And the vessel that he made of clay was marred in the hand of the potter: so he made it again another vessel, as seemed good to the potter to make it."

question: What central theological principle of divine sovereignty does God declare through the potter's work in Jeremiah 18:6?
option1: Can the axe boast itself against him that heweth therewith? or shall the saw magnify itself against him that shaketh it?
option2: Shall the clay say to him that fashioneth it, What makest thou? or thy work, He hath no hands?
option3: Woe unto him that striveth with his Maker! Let the potsherd strive with the potsherds of the earth
option4: O house of Israel, cannot I do with you as this potter? saith the LORD. Behold, as the clay is in the potter's hand, so are ye in mine hand
correct: O house of Israel, cannot I do with you as this potter? saith the LORD. Behold, as the clay is in the potter's hand, so are ye in mine hand
explanation: God asserts His absolute sovereign prerogative over nations: Israel is malleable clay in the hands of the divine Craftsman. Jeremiah 18:6 (KJV) - "O house of Israel, cannot I do with you as this potter? saith the LORD. Behold, as the clay is in the potter's hand, so are ye in mine hand, O house of Israel."

question: What conditional dynamic governs divine decrees of judgment against a nation according to Jeremiah 18:7-8?
option1: If that nation, against whom I have pronounced, turn from their evil, I will repent of the evil that I thought to do unto them
option2: The decree of the Almighty is irrevocable and can never be altered by human tears
option3: Judgment is delayed for forty days, after which the city must be overthrown
option4: Only through the blood of animal sacrifices can the wrath of God be averted
correct: If that nation, against whom I have pronounced, turn from their evil, I will repent of the evil that I thought to do unto them
explanation: Prophetic threats of destruction are conditional: genuine national repentance prompts God to relent of the announced calamity (as witnessed in Nineveh under Jonah). Jeremiah 18:7-8 (KJV) - "At what instant I shall speak concerning a nation, and concerning a kingdom, to pluck up, and to pull down, and to destroy it; If that nation, against whom I have pronounced, turn from their evil, I will repent of the evil that I thought to do unto them."

question: What corresponding conditional dynamic governs divine promises of blessing to a nation according to Jeremiah 18:9-10?
option1: Divine blessings once given can never be revoked because of the oath sworn to Abraham
option2: If it do evil in my sight, that it obey not my voice, then I will repent of the good, wherewith I said I would benefit them
option3: A nation that receives prosperity shall remain fruitful unto a thousand generations
option4: The gifts and calling of God are without repentance regardless of national iniquity
correct: If it do evil in my sight, that it obey not my voice, then I will repent of the good, wherewith I said I would benefit them
explanation: National promises are equally conditional: if a favored people lapses into evil, God withholds the promised prosperity. Jeremiah 18:9-10 (KJV) - "And at what instant I shall speak concerning a nation, and concerning a kingdom, to build and to plant it; If it do evil in my sight, that it obey not my voice, then I will repent of the good, wherewith I said I would benefit them."

question: What fatalistic and defiant response did the people give when urged to turn from their evil ways in Jeremiah 18:12?
option1: The law of Moses is our shield, and no enemy can break the gates of Mount Zion
option2: We have made a covenant with death, and with hell are we at agreement
option3: There is no hope: but we will walk after our own devices, and we will every one do the imagination of his evil heart
option4: Prophesy unto us smooth things, prophesy deceits, and cause the Holy One of Israel to cease
correct: There is no hope: but we will walk after our own devices, and we will every one do the imagination of his evil heart
explanation: Hardened by cynicism and addicted to sin, the people despaired of repentance ('There is no hope' / no'ash) and resolved to persist in their stubborn rebellion. Jeremiah 18:12 (KJV) - "And they said, There is no hope: but we will walk after our own devices, and we will every one do the imagination of his evil heart."

question: What natural consistency in the physical creation shames Israel's unnatural apostasy in Jeremiah 18:14?
option1: Doth the sun forget his rising in the east, or the moon her appointed seasons?
option2: Doth the sea overflow the sandy bounds, or the mountain skip like a ram?
option3: Doth the desert wind cease from blowing, or the clouds withhold the morning dew?
option4: Will a man leave the snow of Lebanon which cometh from the rock of the field? or shall the cold flowing waters that come from another place be forsaken?
correct: Will a man leave the snow of Lebanon which cometh from the rock of the field? or shall the cold flowing waters that come from another place be forsaken?
explanation: Perpetual snows upon Mount Lebanon and cold flowing mountain springs never fail; yet Israel irrationally abandoned her eternal Creator for hollow idols. Jeremiah 18:14 (KJV) - "Will a man leave the snow of Lebanon which cometh from the rock of the field? or shall the cold flowing waters that come from another place be forsaken?"

question: What three religious authorities did the conspirators rally behind when plotting to silence Jeremiah in Jeremiah 18:18?
option1: The priest (the law), the wise (counsel), and the prophet (the word)
option2: The king (the sceptre), the judge (the sword), and the elder (the gate)
option3: The scribe (the pen), the Levite (the altar), and the singer (the psalm)
option4: The soldier (the shield), the captain (the spear), and the archer (the bow)
correct: The priest (the law), the wise (counsel), and the prophet (the word)
explanation: Jerusalem's corrupt religious establishment argued that they possessed all necessary divine guidance - Torah from priests, wisdom from sages, and prophecy from court seers - rendering Jeremiah's message dispensable and treasonous. Jeremiah 18:18 (KJV) - "Then said they, Come, and let us devise devices against Jeremiah; for the law shall not perish from the priest, nor counsel from the wise, nor the word from the prophet. Come, and let us smite him with the tongue, and let us not give heed to any of his words."

question: How did the conspirators plan to destroy Jeremiah in Jeremiah 18:18?
option1: Come, and let us hire assassins from Damascus to murder him in the dark
option2: Come, and let us smite him with the tongue, and let us not give heed to any of his words
option3: Come, and let us cast him into the dungeon of Malchiah to starve
option4: Come, and let us stone him outside the gate of Benjamin as a false prophet
correct: Come, and let us smite him with the tongue, and let us not give heed to any of his words
explanation: They plotted character assassination and legal defamation ('smite him with the tongue') through false accusations to discredit his prophetic ministry before the authorities. Jeremiah 18:18 (KJV) - " ... Come, and let us smite him with the tongue, and let us not give heed to any of his words."

question: What sharp reminder of his past intercessory love did Jeremiah bring before God when praying for justice against his enemies in Jeremiah 18:20?
option1: Remember how I fasted seven days in sackcloth for the healing of Jerusalem
option2: Remember how I wept in secret places while they feasted in their palaces
option3: Remember that I stood before thee to speak good for them, and to turn away thy wrath from them
option4: Remember the covenant thou didst make with me at Anathoth to deliver my life
correct: Remember that I stood before thee to speak good for them, and to turn away thy wrath from them
explanation: Jeremiah laments that they repaid evil for good: while he had stood in the divine council pleading for their preservation, they secretly dug traps to take his life. Jeremiah 18:20 (KJV) - "Shall evil be recompensed for good? for they have digged a pit for my soul. Remember that I stood before thee to speak good for them, and to turn away thy wrath from them."

question: What ceramic vessel was Jeremiah commanded to purchase from a potter and take to the Valley of the son of Hinnom in Jeremiah 19:1-2?
option1: A bronze basin
option2: An alabaster cruse
option3: A potter's earthen bottle
option4: A silver flagon
correct: A potter's earthen bottle
explanation: Jeremiah bought an inexpensive clay water jug ('earthen bottle' / baqbuq), accompanied by elders and senior priests, to the Valley of Hinnom by the Potsherd Gate. Jeremiah 19:1-2 (KJV) - "Thus saith the LORD, Go and get a potter's earthen bottle, and take of the ancients of the people, and of the ancients of the priests; And go forth unto the valley of the son of Hinnom, which is by the entry of the east gate, and proclaim there the words that I shall tell thee,"

question: What physical sensory reaction will seize anyone who hears the catastrophic judgment God will bring upon Jerusalem in Jeremiah 19:3?
option1: His heart shall melt like water
option2: His knees shall smite together
option3: His eyes shall fail with tears
option4: His ears shall tingle
correct: His ears shall tingle
explanation: The shock of Jerusalem's impending demolition will cause the ears of all listeners to ring or vibrate with horror (first used in 1 Samuel 3:11 and 2 Kings 21:12). Jeremiah 19:3 (KJV) - "And say, Hear ye the word of the LORD, O kings of Judah, and inhabitants of Jerusalem; Thus saith the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel; Behold, I will bring evil upon this place, the which whosoever heareth, his ears shall tingle."

question: What unspeakable atrocity of cannibalism during the final Babylonian siege is foretold in Jeremiah 19:9?
option1: I will cause them to eat the flesh of their sons and the flesh of their daughters, and they shall eat every one the flesh of his friend
option2: They shall eat the defiled corpses of the priests and drink the blood of the sacrifices
option3: They shall eat wild herbs and chew on animal skins until pestilence devours them
option4: They shall fight like starving beasts over unclean camel flesh in the marketplace
correct: I will cause them to eat the flesh of their sons and the flesh of their daughters, and they shall eat every one the flesh of his friend
explanation: In fulfillment of Deuteronomy 28:53-57, extreme siege starvation forced trapped inhabitants into horrific familial cannibalism. Jeremiah 19:9 (KJV) - "And I will cause them to eat the flesh of their sons and the flesh of their daughters, and they shall eat every one the flesh of his friend in the siege and straitness, wherewith their enemies, and they that seek their lives, shall straiten them."

question: What dramatic symbolic action was Jeremiah commanded to perform with the earthen bottle before the elders and priests in Jeremiah 19:10-11?
option1: Cast the bottle into the burning flames of Tophet until the clay melts into ashes
option2: Then shalt thou break the bottle in the sight of the men that go with thee, and shalt say unto them ... Even so will I break this people and this city, as one breaketh a potter's vessel, that cannot be made whole again
option3: Bury the bottle in the mud of the valley of Hinnom until the rainy season washes it away
option4: Fill the bottle with bitter waters from the brook Kidron and pour it out upon the threshold
correct: Then shalt thou break the bottle in the sight of the men that go with thee, and shalt say unto them ... Even so will I break this people and this city, as one breaketh a potter's vessel, that cannot be made whole again
explanation: Unlike the malleable clay on the wheel in Chapter 18, a fired ceramic flask once shattered is irreparably destroyed: signifying the irreversible smash of the nation. Jeremiah 19:10-11 (KJV) - "Then shalt thou break the bottle in the sight of the men that go with thee, And shalt say unto them, Thus saith the LORD of hosts; Even so will I break this people and this city, as one breaketh a potter's vessel, that cannot be made whole again: and they shall bury them in Tophet, till there be no place to bury."

question: Why will the private houses of Jerusalem and royal palaces become defiled like the unburied corpses of Tophet in Jeremiah 19:13?
option1: Because they stored stolen wealth and unjust gains in their private chambers
option2: Because they murdered the righteous prophets within their walled courtyards
option3: Because of all the houses upon whose roofs they have burned incense unto all the host of heaven, and have poured out drink offerings unto other gods
option4: Because they built secret chambers of imagery with creeping things and abominable beasts
correct: Because of all the houses upon whose roofs they have burned incense unto all the host of heaven, and have poured out drink offerings unto other gods
explanation: Flat residential rooftops had been converted into open-air astral observatories and pagan altars to worship the sun, moon, and planetary constellations. Jeremiah 19:13 (KJV) - "And the houses of Jerusalem, and the houses of the kings of Judah, shall be defiled as the place of Tophet, because of all the houses upon whose roofs they have burned incense unto all the host of heaven, and have poured out drink offerings unto other gods."

question: Where did Jeremiah stand to deliver his public sermon to all the people immediately upon returning from Tophet in Jeremiah 19:14?
option1: At the East Gate of the city
option2: Before the royal palace of Jehoiakim
option3: In the valley of Jehoshaphat
option4: In the court of the LORD's house
correct: In the court of the LORD's house
explanation: Emerging from the valley of slaughter, Jeremiah boldly strode into the temple courtyard to announce judgment to the assembled worshippers. Jeremiah 19:14 (KJV) - "Then came Jeremiah from Tophet, whither the LORD had sent him to prophesy; and he stood in the court of the LORD's house; and said to all the people,"

question: What anatomical obstinacy caused God to bring all pronounced judgment upon Jerusalem and her towns in Jeremiah 19:15?
option1: Because they have hardened their necks, that they might not hear my words
option2: Because their eyes were blinded by Egyptian promises
option3: Because their hands were defiled with the blood of innocent children
option4: Because their heart was turned to stone by the deceit of false diviners
correct: Because they have hardened their necks, that they might not hear my words
explanation: Like an untamed ox stiffening its neck against the yoke, Judah obstinately hardened her neck against divine warnings. Jeremiah 19:15 (KJV) - "Thus saith the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel; Behold, I will bring upon this city and upon all her towns all the evil that I have pronounced against it, because they have hardened their necks, that they might not hear my words."

question: What new name replacing Tophet and the Valley of Hinnom emphasizes the vast number of casualties in Jeremiah 19:6?
option1: The field of blood
option2: The valley of slaughter
option3: The pit of desolation
option4: The grave of kings
correct: The valley of slaughter
explanation: The valley of Hinnom is prophetically renamed 'The Valley of Slaughter' because dead bodies will be piled there until room for burial runs out. Jeremiah 19:6 (KJV) - "Therefore, behold, the days come, saith the LORD, that this place shall no more be called Tophet, nor The valley of the son of Hinnom, but The valley of slaughter."

question: What mocking reaction will foreign travelers exhibit when passing by the ruins of Jerusalem in Jeremiah 19:8?
option1: They shall clap their hands and weep over her fallen towers
option2: They shall shake their swords and plunder the remaining bronze
option3: Every one that passeth thereby shall be astonished and hiss because of all the plagues thereof
option4: They shall sing a mournful dirge over the virgin of Zion
correct: Every one that passeth thereby shall be astonished and hiss because of all the plagues thereof
explanation: Passersby will gasp in astonishment and hiss in scornful derision at the catastrophic desolation of the once-proud city. Jeremiah 19:8 (KJV) - "And I will make this city desolate, and an hissing; every one that passeth thereby shall be astonished and hiss because of all the plagues thereof."

question: What specific innocent victims filled the Valley of Hinnom through royal Judean sponsorship in Jeremiah 19:4-5?
option1: The righteous prophets murdered by the kings of Judah
option2: The poor and needy defrauded by greedy merchant princes
option3: The foreign strangers enslaved in royal quarries
option4: The blood of innocents, burning their sons with fire for burnt offerings unto Baal
correct: The blood of innocents, burning their sons with fire for burnt offerings unto Baal
explanation: The Valley was saturated with the blood of slaughtered children burned alive in fire rituals dedicated to Baal and Molech. Jeremiah 19:4-5 (KJV) - "Because they have forsaken me ... and have filled this place with the blood of innocents; They have built also the high places of Baal, to burn their sons with fire for burnt offerings unto Baal, which I commanded not, nor spake it, neither came it into my mind:"

question: Who was the chief officer in the temple who struck Jeremiah and incarcerated him in the stocks in Jeremiah 20:1-2?
option1: Zephaniah the son of Maaseiah the priest
option2: Pashur the son of Melchiah the prince
option3: Hilkias the high priest of the sanctuary
option4: Pashur the son of Immer the priest, chief governor in the house of the LORD
correct: Pashur the son of Immer the priest, chief governor in the house of the LORD
explanation: Pashur ben Immer, the chief temple administrator ('chief governor' / paqid nagid), assaulted Jeremiah and locked him in painful public pillory stocks. Jeremiah 20:1-2 (KJV) - "Now Pashur the son of Immer the priest, who was also chief governor in the house of the LORD, heard that Jeremiah prophesied these things. Then Pashur smote Jeremiah the prophet, and put him in the stocks that were in the high gate of Benjamin, which was by the house of the LORD."

question: What ominous symbolic name did Jeremiah bestow upon Pashur upon being released from the stocks in Jeremiah 20:3?
option1: Magormissabib
option2: Ichabod
option3: Lo-ammi
option4: Mahershalalhashbaz
correct: Magormissabib
explanation: Jeremiah renamed Pashur 'Magormissabib' ('Terror on Every Side'), signifying that he would become a living embodiment of terror to himself and his false-prophesying circle. Jeremiah 20:3 (KJV) - "And it came to pass on the morrow, that Pashur brought forth Jeremiah out of the stocks. Then said Jeremiah unto him, The LORD hath not called thy name Pashur, but Magormissabib."

question: What fate did Jeremiah prophesy specifically for Pashur and his household in Jeremiah 20:6?
option1: Thou shalt be slain with the edge of the sword before the high altar of Solomon
option2: Thou shalt come to Babylon, and there thou shalt die, and shalt be buried there, thou, and all thy friends, to whom thou hast prophesied lies
option3: Thou shalt be blinded and cast into the pit of Malchiah to perish of famine
option4: Thou shalt flee into Egypt and be buried in the sands of Tahapanes
correct: Thou shalt come to Babylon, and there thou shalt die, and shalt be buried there, thou, and all thy friends, to whom thou hast prophesied lies
explanation: Pashur would witness the execution of his loved ones, be dragged into Babylonian captivity, and die in foreign exile. Jeremiah 20:6 (KJV) - "And thou, Pashur, and all that dwell in thine house shall go into captivity: and thou shalt come to Babylon, and there thou shalt die, and shalt be buried there, thou, and all thy friends, to whom thou hast prophesied lies."

question: What daring, agonizing accusation of divine overpowering does Jeremiah utter in his private confession in Jeremiah 20:7?
option1: Why hast thou forsaken me in the midst of mine enemies, O God of my salvation?
option2: Thou hast delivered me into the hand of cruel men, and hid thy face from my tears
option3: O LORD, thou hast deceived me, and I was deceived: thou art stronger than I, and hast prevailed: I am in derision daily, every one mocketh me
option4: Hath the Almighty broken his covenant with his anointed servant at the gate of Benjamin?
correct: O LORD, thou hast deceived me, and I was deceived: thou art stronger than I, and hast prevailed: I am in derision daily, every one mocketh me
explanation: Jeremiah pours out raw spiritual angst, feeling seduced and overpowered ('pittitani' - persuaded/overwhelmed) by God into an intolerable vocation of relentless mockery. Jeremiah 20:7 (KJV) - "O LORD, thou hast deceived me, and I was deceived: thou art stronger than I, and hast prevailed: I am in derision daily, every one mocketh me."

question: What two-word summary characterized the core message Jeremiah was compelled to shout, bringing constant reproach upon him in Jeremiah 20:8?
option1: Woe and desolation
option2: Sword and famine
option3: Wrath and fire
option4: Violence and spoil
correct: Violence and spoil
explanation: Jeremiah's message was an agonizing outcry against oppression and impending plunder: 'I cried violence and spoil!' ('chamas vashod'). Jeremiah 20:8 (KJV) - "For since I spake, I cried out, I cried violence and spoil; because the word of the LORD was made a reproach unto me, and a derision, daily."

question: What irresistible internal combustion overwhelmed Jeremiah when he resolved to remain silent and speak no more in God's name in Jeremiah 20:9?
option1: His word was in mine heart as a burning fire shut up in my bones, and I was weary with forbearing, and I could not stay
option2: A mighty whirlwind shook my soul, and an iron hand constrained my lips to open
option3: The Spirit of the LORD fell upon me like lightning, and I trembled exceedingly
option4: A voice like the roar of the sea commanded me to speak before the kings of Judah
correct: His word was in mine heart as a burning fire shut up in my bones, and I was weary with forbearing, and I could not stay
explanation: When Jeremiah tried to resign from prophetic office, God's revelation ignited like trapped volcanic fire in his skeleton: he was powerless to contain it. Jeremiah 20:9 (KJV) - "Then I said, I will not make mention of him, nor speak any more in his name. But his word was in mine heart as a burning fire shut up in my bones, and I was weary with forbearing, and I could not stay."

question: What whispered conspiracy among his close companions ('familiars') did Jeremiah overhear in Jeremiah 20:10?
option1: Let us smite him secretly in the night, and throw his carcass into the brook Kidron
option2: Report, say they, and we will report it. All my familiars watched for my halting, saying, Peradventure he will be enticed, and we shall prevail against him, and we shall take our revenge on him
option3: Let us bribe the false witnesses to swear treason against the life of the king
option4: Let us deliver him to Pashur the priest that his name may be blotted out forever
correct: Report, say they, and we will report it. All my familiars watched for my halting, saying, Peradventure he will be enticed, and we shall prevail against him, and we shall take our revenge on him
explanation: Jeremiah's former trusted associates turned into spies, stalking his every step and waiting for a slip of the tongue to denounce him for treason. Jeremiah 20:10 (KJV) - "For I heard the defaming of many, fear on every side. Report, say they, and we will report it. All my familiars watched for my halting, saying, Peradventure he will be enticed, and we shall prevail against him, and we shall take our revenge on him."

question: What military title of supreme confidence does Jeremiah ascribe to God as his personal champion in Jeremiah 20:11?
option1: The Lord of Hosts
option2: A captain of the host
option3: A mighty terrible one
option4: The King of Glory
correct: A mighty terrible one
explanation: Jeremiah rallies his faith: Yahweh stands beside him as an invincible, terrifying warrior ('gibbor arits'), guaranteeing the downfall of his persecutors. Jeremiah 20:11 (KJV) - "But the LORD is with me as a mighty terrible one: therefore my persecutors shall stumble, and they shall not prevail: they shall be greatly ashamed; for they shall not prosper: their everlasting confusion shall never be forgotten."

question: What sudden emotional oscillation carries Jeremiah from praising God in verse 13 into profound despair in Jeremiah 20:14?
option1: Woe is me that I dwell in the tents of Kedar and wander in the wilderness
option2: O that I had wings like a dove! for then would I fly away, and be at rest
option3: My soul melteth for heaviness: strengthen thou me according unto thy word
option4: Cursed be the day wherein I was born: let not the day wherein my mother bare me be blessed
correct: Cursed be the day wherein I was born: let not the day wherein my mother bare me be blessed
explanation: Echoing Job 3, Jeremiah experiences a dramatic plunge from spiritual victory into the dark night of the soul, cursing the very calendar day of his birth. Jeremiah 20:14 (KJV) - "Cursed be the day wherein I was born: let not the day wherein my mother bare me be blessed."

question: Who does Jeremiah curse in Jeremiah 20:15-16, wishing him to hear battle cries at noontide?
option1: The man who brought tidings to my father, saying, A man child is born unto thee; making him very glad
option2: Pashur the priest who smote him in the house of the LORD
option3: The false prophets who prophesied peace unto the house of David
option4: The kings of Judah who burned incense upon the roofs of Jerusalem
correct: The man who brought tidings to my father, saying, A man child is born unto thee; making him very glad
explanation: Jeremiah vents grief upon the anonymous courier who brought joyful birth announcements to his father Hilkiah, wishing him the fate of Sodom and Gomorrah. Jeremiah 20:15-16 (KJV) - "Cursed be the man who brought tidings to my father, saying, A man child is born unto thee; making him very glad. And let that man be as the cities which the LORD overthrew, and repented not: and let him hear the cry in the morning, and the shouting at noontide;"

question: Which two royal delegates did King Zedekiah dispatch to Jeremiah to inquire whether God would intervene against Nebuchadnezzar in Jeremiah 21:1-2?
option1: Pashur the son of Melchiah, and Zephaniah the son of Maaseiah the priest
option2: Shaphan the scribe, and Hilkiah the high priest
option3: Ebed-melech the Ethiopian, and Baruch the son of Neriah
option4: Gedaliah the son of Ahikam, and Ishmael the son of Nethaniah
correct: Pashur the son of Melchiah, and Zephaniah the son of Maaseiah the priest
explanation: King Zedekiah sent a high-level embassy comprising Prince Pashur ben Melchiah and Priest Zephaniah ben Maaseiah to ask for a miracle similar to Hezekiah's deliverance. Jeremiah 21:1-2 (KJV) - "The word which came unto Jeremiah from the LORD, when king Zedekiah sent unto him Pashur the son of Melchiah, and Zephaniah the son of Maaseiah the priest, saying, Enquire, I pray thee, of the LORD for us; for Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon maketh war against us; if so be that the LORD will deal with us according to all his wondrous works, that he may go up from us."

question: What terrifying military reversal did God announce against Judah's defense forces in Jeremiah 21:4?
option1: I will break the bows of your mighty men and cause your chariots to sink into the mire
option2: Behold, I will turn back the weapons of war that are in your hands ... and I will assemble them into the midst of this city
option3: I will send an angel to blind your captains and scatter your archers upon the mountains
option4: I will cause your swords to turn against your brethren until no warrior remaineth
correct: Behold, I will turn back the weapons of war that are in your hands ... and I will assemble them into the midst of this city
explanation: God declared that Judean weapons would backfire and be forced inward, assembling the retreating defenders trapped inside the doomed urban core. Jeremiah 21:4 (KJV) - "Thus saith the LORD God of Israel; Behold, I will turn back the weapons of war that are in your hands, wherewith ye fight against the king of Babylon, and against the Chaldeans, which besiege you without the walls, and I will assemble them into the midst of this city."

question: What astonishing declaration transforms Yahweh from Israel's traditional Protector into her supreme Adversary in Jeremiah 21:5?
option1: I will withdraw my presence from the mercy seat and watch your destruction from afar
option2: I will deliver you to the King of the North as a servant delivereth a broken vessel
option3: And I myself will fight against you with an outstretched hand and with a strong arm, even in anger, and in fury, and in great wrath
option4: I will command the host of heaven to pour down brimstone upon your towers
correct: And I myself will fight against you with an outstretched hand and with a strong arm, even in anger, and in fury, and in great wrath
explanation: The sacred Exodus formula ('with an outstretched hand and strong arm', traditionally used of delivering Israel from Pharaoh) is shocking: God now deploys that same omnipotent arm to war against Judah! Jeremiah 21:5 (KJV) - "And I myself will fight against you with an outstretched hand and with a strong arm, even in anger, and in fury, and in great wrath."

question: What two stark alternatives does God place before the besieged population in Jeremiah 21:8?
option1: The way of the blessing, and the way of the curse
option2: The way of the covenant, and the way of the heathen
option3: The way of holiness, and the way of transgression
option4: Behold, I set before you the way of life, and the way of death
correct: Behold, I set before you the way of life, and the way of death
explanation: Jeremiah sets before them a life-or-death ultimatum reminiscent of Deuteronomy 30:19, challenging individual citizens to make their personal choice. Jeremiah 21:8 (KJV) - "And unto this people thou shalt say, Thus saith the LORD; Behold, I set before you the way of life, and the way of death."

question: What is the counterintuitive 'way of life' commanded by God in Jeremiah 21:9?
option1: He that goeth out, and falleth to the Chaldeans that besiege you, he shall live, and his life shall be unto him for a prey
option2: He that fasteth seven days in the temple and prayeth before the Ark of the Covenant
option3: He that escapeth through the secret water tunnels into the desert of Engedi
option4: He that fighteth valiantly upon the battlements of Zion until the morning
correct: He that goeth out, and falleth to the Chaldeans that besiege you, he shall live, and his life shall be unto him for a prey
explanation: Surrendering (deserting) to the Babylonian forces was paradoxical divine wisdom: those who submitted would escape death and walk away with their bare lives ('life as a prey'). Jeremiah 21:9 (KJV) - "He that abideth in this city shall die by the sword, and by the famine, and by the pestilence: but he that goeth out, and falleth to the Chaldeans that besiege you, he shall live, and his life shall be unto him for a prey."

question: What guaranteed destruction awaits those who stubbornly remain inside the city in Jeremiah 21:9-10?
option1: They shall be sold as slaves to Egypt and their inheritance confiscated
option2: He that abideth in this city shall die by the sword, and by the famine, and by the pestilence ... it shall be given into the hand of the king of Babylon, and he shall burn it with fire
option3: They shall be carried away into the mountains of Media and forgotten
option4: They shall wander as blind beggars among the ruins of the temple
correct: He that abideth in this city shall die by the sword, and by the famine, and by the pestilence ... it shall be given into the hand of the king of Babylon, and he shall burn it with fire
explanation: Remaining in Jerusalem was suicide: resistance guaranteed death by war, starvation, or plague, ending with the entire city incinerated. Jeremiah 21:9-10 (KJV) - "He that abideth in this city shall die by the sword, and by the famine, and by the pestilence ... For I have set my face against this city for evil, and not for good, saith the LORD: it shall be given into the hand of the king of Babylon, and he shall burn it with fire."

question: What morning civic responsibility was commanded to the royal house of David to avert divine fury in Jeremiah 21:12?
option1: Offer the daily morning burnt offering upon the bronze altar with solemn prayer
option2: Inspect the city walls and review the armed guards at the water gates
option3: Execute judgment in the morning, and deliver him that is spoiled out of the hand of the oppressor
option4: Distribute royal bread and oil to the widows and orphans of Jerusalem
correct: Execute judgment in the morning, and deliver him that is spoiled out of the hand of the oppressor
explanation: Davidic monarchs were obligated to open morning court sessions at the city gate to ensure swift judicial relief for defrauded victims of oppression. Jeremiah 21:12 (KJV) - "O house of David, thus saith the LORD; Execute judgment in the morning, and deliver him that is spoiled out of the hand of the oppressor, lest my fury go out like fire, and burn that none can quench it, because of the evil of your doings."

question: What boastful, false security of Jerusalem's mountain topography does God shatter in Jeremiah 21:13?
option1: Which say, The mountains are round about Jerusalem, so the LORD is round about his people
option2: Which say, Our walls are built upon the rocky crags that no siege engine can shake
option3: Which say, We have deep cisterns of water and royal storehouses of grain for twenty years
option4: Which say, Who shall come down against us? or who shall enter into our habitations?
correct: Which say, Who shall come down against us? or who shall enter into our habitations?
explanation: Jerusalem fancied herself an impregnable mountain redoubt ('inhabitant of the valley, and rock of the plain'), falsely boasting that no conqueror could breach her ravines. Jeremiah 21:13 (KJV) - "Behold, I am against thee, O inhabitant of the valley, and rock of the plain, saith the LORD; which say, Who shall come down against us? or who shall enter into our habitations?"

question: What fate will overtake King Zedekiah and the royal survivors according to Jeremiah 21:7?
option1: I will deliver Zedekiah ... into the hand of Nebuchadrezzar ... and he shall smite them with the edge of the sword; he shall not spare them, neither have pity, nor have mercy
option2: He shall die in peace in his own bed, and men shall lament for him with royal perfumes
option3: He shall flee across the Jordan and be protected by the king of the Ammonites
option4: He shall be restored to his throne after paying tribute of ten talents of gold
correct: I will deliver Zedekiah ... into the hand of Nebuchadrezzar ... and he shall smite them with the edge of the sword; he shall not spare them, neither have pity, nor have mercy
explanation: Zedekiah and his entourage would experience ruthless Babylonian vengeance without mercy (culminating in Riblah where his sons were slaughtered before his eyes). Jeremiah 21:7 (KJV) - "And afterward, saith the LORD, I will deliver Zedekiah king of Judah, and his servants, and the people ... into the hand of Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon ... and he shall smite them with the edge of the sword; he shall not spare them, neither have pity, nor have mercy."

question: What forest metaphor describes the destruction of Jerusalem's lavish cedar palaces in Jeremiah 21:14?
option1: I will send an army of woodcutters with axes to fell every noble cedar
option2: I will kindle a fire in the forest thereof, and it shall devour all things round about it
option3: I will uproot the trees of the garden and cast them into the dry brook
option4: I will strip off the branches and leave only barren stumps in the earth
correct: I will kindle a fire in the forest thereof, and it shall devour all things round about it
explanation: Jerusalem's luxurious cedar-paneled palaces (such as the House of the Forest of Lebanon) are viewed as dense timber fuel for an uncontrollable conflagration. Jeremiah 21:14 (KJV) - "But I will punish you according to the fruit of your doings, saith the LORD: and I will kindle a fire in the forest thereof, and it shall devour all things round about it."

question: For which royal prince does Jeremiah command the nation to 'weep sore', because he would die in foreign captivity and never see his homeland again in Jeremiah 22:10-12?
option1: Jehoiakim the son of Josiah
option2: Shallum (Jehoahaz) the son of Josiah
option3: Zedekiah the son of Josiah
option4: Coniah the son of Jehoiakim
correct: Shallum (Jehoahaz) the son of Josiah
explanation: Shallum (Jehoahaz) reigned for only three months in 609 BC before being deposed and exiled to Egypt by Pharaoh Necho, never to return. Jeremiah 22:11-12 (KJV) - "For thus saith the LORD touching Shallum the son of Josiah king of Judah, which reigned instead of Josiah his father, which went forth out of this place; He shall not return thither any more: But he shall die in the place whither they have led him captive, and shall see this land no more."

question: What sharp condemnation does Jeremiah pronounce against King Jehoiakim for his exploitative palace construction in Jeremiah 22:13-14?
option1: Woe unto him that layeth foundation stones with the blood of innocent children and setteth up gates with silver
option2: Woe unto him that melteth the sacred vessels of the temple to overlay his private throne with gold
option3: Woe unto him that buildeth his house by unrighteousness, and his chambers by wrong; that useth his neighbour's service without wages, and giveth him not for his work
option4: Woe unto him that enforceth heavy taxes upon the poor while drinking wine in large bowls
correct: Woe unto him that buildeth his house by unrighteousness, and his chambers by wrong; that useth his neighbour's service without wages, and giveth him not for his work
explanation: During national economic distress, King Jehoiakim indulged in extravagant palace expansions using forced, unpaid domestic labor. Jeremiah 22:13 (KJV) - "Woe unto him that buildeth his house by unrighteousness, and his chambers by wrong; that useth his neighbour's service without wages, and giveth him not for his work;"

question: What luxurious architectural features did Jehoiakim boast of in his unrighteous royal palace in Jeremiah 22:14?
option1: High towers of polished marble, gates of hammered brass, and floors of ivory
option2: A throne room overlaid with gold of Ophir, and hung with royal purple tapestries
option3: Carved pillars of granite, hanging gardens of exotic flowers, and silver fountains
option4: A wide house and large chambers, cutteth him out windows; and it is cieled with cedar, and painted with vermilion
correct: A wide house and large chambers, cutteth him out windows; and it is cieled with cedar, and painted with vermilion
explanation: Jehoiakim spent public funds on expansive cedar paneling and imported brilliant red pigment (vermilion / shashar). Jeremiah 22:14 (KJV) - "That saith, I will build me a wide house and large chambers, and cutteth him out windows; and it is cieled with cedar, and painted with vermilion."

question: How did God contrast Jehoiakim's vanity with the authentic godly reign of his father King Josiah in Jeremiah 22:15-16?
option1: Did not thy father eat and drink, and do judgment and justice, and then it was well with him? He judged the cause of the poor and needy ... was not this to know me? saith the LORD
option2: Did not thy father fast forty days and rebuild the walls of the city in righteousness?
option3: Did not thy father assemble all Israel to swear by the covenant on Mount Gerizim?
option4: Did not thy father destroy the chariots of the sun and slay the priests of Baal?
correct: Did not thy father eat and drink, and do judgment and justice, and then it was well with him? He judged the cause of the poor and needy ... was not this to know me? saith the LORD
explanation: True knowledge of God is defined not by theological slogans or cedar palaces, but by practicing social justice and defending vulnerable widows, orphans, and the poor. Jeremiah 22:15-16 (KJV) - "Shalt thou reign, because thou closest thyself in cedar? did not thy father eat and drink, and do judgment and justice, and then it was well with him? He judged the cause of the poor and needy; then it was well with him: was not this to know me? saith the LORD."

question: What ignominious, unlamented funeral awaits King Jehoiakim in Jeremiah 22:18-19?
option1: He shall be burned in the valley of Tophet with the carcases of unclean beasts
option2: He shall be buried with the burial of an ass, drawn and cast forth beyond the gates of Jerusalem
option3: He shall be cast into the dry pit of Malchiah without a shroud or spices
option4: He shall be devoured by street dogs outside the Water Gate before his servants
correct: He shall be buried with the burial of an ass, drawn and cast forth beyond the gates of Jerusalem
explanation: Denied royal mourning rites ('Ah lord! or, Ah his glory!'), Jehoiakim's corpse will be dragged like dead animal carrion and discarded outside the city walls. Jeremiah 22:19 (KJV) - "He shall be buried with the burial of an ass, drawn and cast forth beyond the gates of Jerusalem."

question: What metaphor of intimate royal authority does God use to declare the absolute rejection of King Coniah (Jehoiachin) in Jeremiah 22:24?
option1: Though he were the crown of gold upon my head, I would cast it into the mire
option2: Though he were the golden sceptre in my palace, I would break it in pieces
option3: Though Coniah the son of Jehoiakim king of Judah were the signet upon my right hand, yet would I pluck thee thence
option4: Though he were the precious jewel upon my breastplate, I would grind it to powder
correct: Though Coniah the son of Jehoiakim king of Judah were the signet upon my right hand, yet would I pluck thee thence
explanation: A signet ring (chotam) was an ancient king's most treasured legal instrument; God declares that even if Coniah occupied that supreme place of favor, He would tear him off and discard him. Jeremiah 22:24 (KJV) - "As I live, saith the LORD, though Coniah the son of Jehoiakim king of Judah were the signet upon my right hand, yet would I pluck thee thence;"

question: To what worthless broken household object does Jeremiah compare deposed King Coniah in Jeremiah 22:28?
option1: A cracked lamp that giveth no light in the darkness
option2: A broken water jar that can hold no wine
option3: A ruined garment cast upon the dungheap
option4: A despised broken idol ... a vessel wherein is no pleasure
correct: A despised broken idol ... a vessel wherein is no pleasure
explanation: Deposed young Jehoiachin was discarded into exile like cheap, cracked pottery ('a vessel wherein is no pleasure' / keli ein chefets bo). Jeremiah 22:28 (KJV) - "Is this man Coniah a despised broken idol? is he a vessel wherein is no pleasure? wherefore are they cast out, he and his seed, and are cast into a land which they know not?"

question: What solemn threefold cosmic summons calls the entire planet to witness the divine judicial sentence upon Coniah in Jeremiah 22:29?
option1: O earth, earth, earth, hear the word of the LORD
option2: Hear, O heavens, and give ear, O earth: for the LORD hath spoken
option3: Awake, awake, O earth: behold the judgment of the King of nations
option4: Tremble, thou earth, at the presence of the Lord, at the presence of the God of Jacob
correct: O earth, earth, earth, hear the word of the LORD
explanation: The majestic threefold repetition of 'Earth' (erets, erets, erets) emphasizes the irrevocable, momentous legal finality of the royal decree. Jeremiah 22:29 (KJV) - "O earth, earth, earth, hear the word of the LORD."

question: What dynastic curse was pronounced upon King Coniah regarding his biological descendants sitting upon David's throne in Jeremiah 22:30?
option1: His sons shall be slain by the sword in Babylon and his daughters carried into Media
option2: Write ye this man childless, a man that shall not prosper in his days: for no man of his seed shall prosper, sitting upon the throne of David, and ruling any more in Judah
option3: His lineage shall be blotted out from the genealogical registers of the priests
option4: His throne shall be given to a stranger from the house of Ephraim forever
correct: Write ye this man childless, a man that shall not prosper in his days: for no man of his seed shall prosper, sitting upon the throne of David, and ruling any more in Judah
explanation: Though Coniah had biological children (1 Chronicles 3:17-18; Matthew 1:12), none of his physical offspring would ever successfully reign as an anointed king on David's throne in Judah. Jeremiah 22:30 (KJV) - "Thus saith the LORD, Write ye this man childless, a man that shall not prosper in his days: for no man of his seed shall prosper, sitting upon the throne of David, and ruling any more in Judah."

question: What geographic and forestry titles are affectionately bestowed upon the royal house of Judah before its destruction in Jeremiah 22:6?
option1: Thou art the rose of Sharon, and the lily of the valleys
option2: Thou art the vineyard of Engedi, and the palm grove of Jericho
option3: Thou art Gilead unto me, and the head of Lebanon
option4: Thou art the garden of Eden, and the mountain of spices
correct: Thou art Gilead unto me, and the head of Lebanon
explanation: Gilead's rich pastures and Lebanon's majestic cedar forests symbolized the royal palace's supreme nobility and wealth before God flattened it into a wilderness. Jeremiah 22:6 (KJV) - "For thus saith the LORD unto the king's house of Judah; Thou art Gilead unto me, and the head of Lebanon: yet surely I will make thee a wilderness, and cities which are not inhabited."

question: What woe is pronounced against Judah's irresponsible political and religious leaders in Jeremiah 23:1-2?
option1: Woe unto the shepherds of Israel that do feed themselves and clothe themselves with the wool!
option2: Woe unto the false guides who lead my flock into the desert to be devoured by wolves!
option3: Woe be unto the pastors that destroy and scatter the sheep of my pasture! ... Ye have scattered my flock, and driven them away, and have not visited them: behold, I will visit upon you the evil of your doings
option4: Woe unto the hirelings who flee when the lion cometh and leave the sheep defenseless!
correct: Woe be unto the pastors that destroy and scatter the sheep of my pasture! ... Ye have scattered my flock, and driven them away, and have not visited them: behold, I will visit upon you the evil of your doings
explanation: God plays on the Hebrew verb paqad ('visit'): because negligent shepherds failed to care for ('visit') His sheep, God will 'visit' punitive judgment upon them. Jeremiah 23:1-2 (KJV) - "Woe be unto the pastors that destroy and scatter the sheep of my pasture! saith the LORD. Therefore thus saith the LORD God of Israel against the pastors that feed my people; Ye have scattered my flock, and driven them away, and have not visited them: behold, I will visit upon you the evil of your doings, saith the LORD."

question: What glorious Messianic title and lineage does God promise to raise up unto David in Jeremiah 23:5?
option1: A prince of peace, whose throne shall be established upon Mount Zion forever
option2: A suffering servant, who shall bear the iniquities of his people in silence
option3: A rod from the stem of Jesse, endowed with the sevenfold spirit of wisdom
option4: A righteous Branch, and a King shall reign and prosper, and shall execute judgment and justice in the earth
correct: A righteous Branch, and a King shall reign and prosper, and shall execute judgment and justice in the earth
explanation: In place of corrupt puppet kings, God promises the Davidic Messiah: 'A righteous Branch' (Tsemach Tsaddiq) who will reign with consummate justice and prosperity. Jeremiah 23:5 (KJV) - "Behold, the days come, saith the LORD, that I will raise unto David a righteous Branch, and a King shall reign and prosper, and shall execute judgment and justice in the earth."

question: What sublime covenant name will be given to this righteous Davidic King in Jeremiah 23:6?
option1: THE LORD OUR RIGHTEOUSNESS
option2: IMMANUEL GOD WITH US
option3: THE EVERLASTING FATHER
option4: THE PRINCE OF SALVATION
correct: THE LORD OUR RIGHTEOUSNESS
explanation: The Messiah is designated 'YAHWEH TSIDQENU' ('THE LORD OUR RIGHTEOUSNESS'), establishing that divine righteousness itself is incarnated and imparted through Him (contrasting King Zedekiah, whose name meant 'My righteousness is Yahweh' but whose reign was wicked). Jeremiah 23:6 (KJV) - "In his days Judah shall be saved, and Israel shall dwell safely: and this is his name whereby he shall be called, THE LORD OUR RIGHTEOUSNESS."

question: To which infamous ancient destroyed cities does God compare the corrupt prophets and inhabitants of Jerusalem in Jeremiah 23:14?
option1: They are as Babylon the mother of harlots, and Nineveh the bloody city
option2: They are all of them unto me as Sodom, and the inhabitants thereof as Gomorrah
option3: They are as Tyre that trusted in her ships, and Sidon that perished in pride
option4: They are as Admah and Zeboim, overthrown in the morning of wrath
correct: They are all of them unto me as Sodom, and the inhabitants thereof as Gomorrah
explanation: Because Jerusalem's false prophets committed adultery, walked in lies, and encouraged evildoers, God evaluated them as morally equivalent to Sodom and Gomorrah. Jeremiah 23:14 (KJV) - "I have seen also in the prophets of Jerusalem an horrible thing: they commit adultery, and walk in lies: they strengthen also the hands of evildoers, that none doth return from his wickedness: they are all of them unto me as Sodom, and the inhabitants thereof as Gomorrah."

question: What false, tranquilizing promise did the deceptive prophets continuously preach to those who despised God in Jeremiah 23:17?
option1: The temple of Solomon shall stand as an iron fortress against the king of Babylon
option2: Pharaoh shall bring horses and chariots to deliver Zion before the new moon
option3: The LORD hath said, Ye shall have peace; and they say unto every one that walketh after the imagination of his own heart, No evil shall come upon you
option4: The exiles shall return with songs of joy within two full years
correct: The LORD hath said, Ye shall have peace; and they say unto every one that walketh after the imagination of his own heart, No evil shall come upon you
explanation: False prophets coddled stubborn sinners with cheap grace: promising unconditional peace ('Shalom') and immunity from judgment. Jeremiah 23:17 (KJV) - "They say still unto them that despise me, The LORD hath said, Ye shall have peace; and they say unto every one that walketh after the imagination of his own heart, No evil shall come upon you."

question: What dual rhetorical questions affirm God's omnipresence and divine transcendence over the universe in Jeremiah 23:23-24?
option1: Where is the house that ye build unto me? and where is the place of my rest? hath not my hand made all these things?
option2: Who hath directed the Spirit of the LORD, or being his counsellor hath taught him? with whom took he counsel?
option3: Can a man hide from the fiery eyes of the Almighty, or flee from the breath of his nostrils?
option4: Am I a God at hand, saith the LORD, and not a God afar off? Can any hide himself in secret places that I shall not see him? saith the LORD. Do not I fill heaven and earth?
correct: Am I a God at hand, saith the LORD, and not a God afar off? Can any hide himself in secret places that I shall not see him? saith the LORD. Do not I fill heaven and earth?
explanation: God shatters pagan local-deity misconceptions: He is neither confined to Jerusalem's temple nor distant in the heavens, but omnipresent, filling all creation. Jeremiah 23:23-24 (KJV) - "Am I a God at hand, saith the LORD, and not a God afar off? Can any hide himself in secret places that I shall not see him? saith the LORD. Do not I fill heaven and earth? saith the LORD."

question: What agricultural contrast distinguishes human dreams and falsehood from genuine divine revelation in Jeremiah 23:28?
option1: What is the chaff to the wheat? saith the LORD
option2: What is the thorn to the noble vine?
option3: What is the bitter gourd to the sweet pomegranate?
option4: What is the worthless tare to the finest grain of Bashan?
correct: What is the chaff to the wheat? saith the LORD
explanation: Human nocturnal fantasies are worthless, empty husks ('chaff'); divine revelation is rich, life-giving, nourishing grain ('wheat'). Jeremiah 23:28 (KJV) - "The prophet that hath a dream, let him tell a dream; and he that hath my word, let him speak my word faithfully. What is the chaff to the wheat? saith the LORD."

question: What two powerful physical metaphors describe the consuming and pulverizing authority of God's word in Jeremiah 23:29?
option1: Is not my word like a sharp twoedged sword, and like a consuming flood of waters?
option2: Is not my word like as a fire? saith the LORD; and like a hammer that breaketh the rock in pieces?
option3: Is not my word like a blazing lightning bolt, and like an iron battering ram?
option4: Is not my word like a roaring lion, and like an unshakeable anvil?
correct: Is not my word like as a fire? saith the LORD; and like a hammer that breaketh the rock in pieces?
explanation: God's word possesses dual supernatural power: it burns away dross like an intense refining fire, and shatters hard-hearted obstinacy like a blacksmith's sledgehammer. Jeremiah 23:29 (KJV) - "Is not my word like as a fire? saith the LORD; and like a hammer that breaketh the rock in pieces?"

question: What plagiarism and rhetorical manipulation does God condemn among the false prophets in Jeremiah 23:30-31?
option1: That sell their visions for silver and divine for handfuls of barley
option2: That alter the words of the book of the law found in the temple
option3: I am against the prophets ... that steal my words every one from his neighbour ... that use their tongues, and say, He saith
option4: That copy the omens of the Chaldeans and inscribe them on scrolls
correct: I am against the prophets ... that steal my words every one from his neighbour ... that use their tongues, and say, He saith
explanation: Lacking authentic divine encounter, false prophets plagiarized phrases from true prophets or mimicked one another, smoothly prefacing their own inventions with a pious 'He saith'. Jeremiah 23:30-31 (KJV) - "Therefore, behold, I am against the prophets, saith the LORD, that steal my words every one from his neighbour. Behold, I am against the prophets, saith the LORD, that use their tongues, and say, He saith."

question: What Hebrew wordplay on 'burden' (massa) results in a total ban on the flippant phrase 'The burden of the LORD' in Jeremiah 23:33-36?
option1: The word 'burden' was reserved exclusively for the high priest on the Day of Atonement
option2: The phrase was borrowed from the Babylonian astrologers who worshipped the heavy stars
option3: The word 'burden' was associated with the tribute of gold paid to Pharaoh Necho
option4: They used 'burden' flippantly to mock prophetic oracles; God replied that the people themselves had become an intolerable burden that He would cast off
correct: They used 'burden' flippantly to mock prophetic oracles; God replied that the people themselves had become an intolerable burden that He would cast off
explanation: The Hebrew word 'massa' meant both a prophetic 'oracle' and a heavy physical 'load/burden'; skeptics sneered, 'What's the burden today?', so God retorted that they had become a weary burden He would cast into exile. Jeremiah 23:33, 36 (KJV) - "And when this people, or the prophet, or a priest, shall ask thee, saying, What is the burden of the LORD? thou shalt then say unto them, What burden? I will even forsake you, saith the LORD ... And the burden of the LORD shall ye mention no more: for every man's word shall be his burden; for ye have perverted the words of the living God, of the LORD of hosts our God."

question: What visionary agricultural display was set before the temple of the LORD in Jeremiah 24:1?
option1: Two clusters of grapes
option2: Two sheaves of barley
option3: Two bowls of pomegranates
option4: Two baskets of figs
correct: Two baskets of figs
explanation: Jeremiah was shown two baskets of figs placed in front of the temple sanctuary after King Jehoiachin and skilled artisans were deported in 597 BC. Jeremiah 24:1 (KJV) - "The LORD shewed me, and, behold, two baskets of figs were set before the temple of the LORD, after that Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon had carried away captive Jeconiah the son of Jehoiakim king of Judah, and the princes of Judah, with the carpenters and smiths, from Jerusalem, and had brought them to Babylon."

question: How were the quality of the two baskets of figs contrasted in Jeremiah 24:2?
option1: One basket had very good figs, even like the figs that are first ripe: and the other basket had very naughty figs, which could not be eaten, they were so bad
option2: One basket was full of sweet green figs, and the other full of dried wild figs
option3: One basket was harvested in spring, and the other gathered after the winter frost
option4: One basket was blessed by the priests, and the other offered unto the queen of heaven
correct: One basket had very good figs, even like the figs that are first ripe: and the other basket had very naughty figs, which could not be eaten, they were so bad
explanation: One basket contained prime first-ripe spring delicacies (bikkurot); the other was packed with rotten, putrid, inedible cullings ('very naughty figs'). Jeremiah 24:2 (KJV) - "One basket had very good figs, even like the figs that are first ripe: and the other basket had very naughty figs, which could not be eaten, they were so bad."

question: Whom did the basket of 'very good figs' represent according to divine revelation in Jeremiah 24:5?
option1: The righteous priests and Levites who ministered faithfully at the altar in Jerusalem
option2: The exiles carried away captive of Judah into the land of the Chaldeans for their good
option3: The poor laborers and vinedressers left behind in the fields of Judah
option4: The faithful remnant who fled into Egypt under the protection of Pharaoh
correct: The exiles carried away captive of Judah into the land of the Chaldeans for their good
explanation: Surprisingly, the elite exiles already deported to Babylon in 597 BC (including Daniel and Ezekiel) were designated 'good figs', whom God sent into exile for their ultimate spiritual preservation. Jeremiah 24:5 (KJV) - "Thus saith the LORD, the God of Israel; Like these good figs, so will I acknowledge them that are carried away captive of Judah, whom I have sent out of this place into the land of the Chaldeans for their good."

question: What three constructive promises does God make concerning the 'good fig' Babylonian exiles in Jeremiah 24:6?
option1: I will give them silver and gold, make them rulers in Babylon, and send angels to guide their steps
option2: I will rebuild the temple within two years, restore the golden ark, and defeat Nebuchadnezzar
option3: I will bring them again to this land: and I will build them, and not pull them down; and I will plant them, and not pluck them up
option4: I will multiply their flocks tenfold, crown their princes with glory, and subdue the nations under them
correct: I will bring them again to this land: and I will build them, and not pull them down; and I will plant them, and not pluck them up
explanation: God promises repatriation and permanent establishment, using the constructive verbs of Jeremiah 1:10: building and planting them in the land. Jeremiah 24:6 (KJV) - "For I will set mine eyes upon them for good, and I will bring them again to this land: and I will build them, and not pull them down; and I will plant them, and not pluck them up."

question: What profound internal spiritual transformation does God promise to bestow upon the exilic remnant in Jeremiah 24:7?
option1: I will give them the tongues of angels to declare my glory among the Chaldeans
option2: I will take away their poverty and make them rich merchants in the cities of the east
option3: I will write the Torah on golden tablets and place it in their hands forever
option4: And I will give them an heart to know me, that I am the LORD: and they shall be my people, and I will be their God: for they shall return unto me with their whole heart
correct: And I will give them an heart to know me, that I am the LORD: and they shall be my people, and I will be their God: for they shall return unto me with their whole heart
explanation: Exile served as a refining furnace: God promised inward heart renewal to genuinely know Yahweh, culminating in wholehearted covenant restoration. Jeremiah 24:7 (KJV) - "And I will give them an heart to know me, that I am the LORD: and they shall be my people, and I will be their God: for they shall return unto me with their whole heart."

question: Whom did the basket of 'very evil figs' represent in Jeremiah 24:8?
option1: Zedekiah the king of Judah, and his princes, and the residue of Jerusalem, that remain in this land, and them that dwell in the land of Egypt
option2: The invading Chaldean army and the generals of Nebuchadnezzar
option3: The false prophets of Babylon who prophesied lies to the exiles
option4: The surrounding pagan nations of Edom, Moab, and Ammon
correct: Zedekiah the king of Judah, and his princes, and the residue of Jerusalem, that remain in this land, and them that dwell in the land of Egypt
explanation: The rotten figs symbolized King Zedekiah, the remnant remaining in Jerusalem who fancied themselves God's favored survivors, and those who sought refuge in Egypt. Jeremiah 24:8 (KJV) - "And as the evil figs, which cannot be eaten, they are so evil; surely thus saith the LORD, So will I give Zedekiah the king of Judah, and his princes, and the residue of Jerusalem, that remain in this land, and them that dwell in the land of Egypt:"

question: What four bywords of international disgrace will attach to the 'evil figs' in all places of their dispersion in Jeremiah 24:9?
option1: A sorrow and an astonishment, a hissing and a desolation
option2: A reproach and a proverb, a taunt and a curse
option3: A parable and a byword, an abomination and a mockery
option4: A lamentation and a tragedy, a warning and a shame
correct: A reproach and a proverb, a taunt and a curse
explanation: Those who resisted God's counsel will become objects of universal ridicule and mockery: a reproach, a proverbial joke, a biting taunt, and a formulaic curse. Jeremiah 24:9 (KJV) - "And I will deliver them to be removed into all the kingdoms of the earth for their hurt, to be a reproach and a proverb, a taunt and a curse, in all places whither I shall drive them."

question: What three divine judgments will pursue the remaining 'evil figs' until they are completely consumed from the promised land in Jeremiah 24:10?
option1: The drought, the mildew, and the locust
option2: The wild beasts, the burning heat, and the sandstorm
option3: The sword, the famine, and the pestilence
option4: The iron chains, the deep pit, and the bitter waters
correct: The sword, the famine, and the pestilence
explanation: The deadly triad - sword, famine, and pestilence - will pursue the rebellious survivors until they are utterly eradicated from the land. Jeremiah 24:10 (KJV) - "And I will send the sword, the famine, and the pestilence, among them, till they be consumed from off the land that I gave unto them and to their fathers."

question: Which professional classes were specifically deported alongside King Jeconiah (Jehoiachin) in 597 BC according to Jeremiah 24:1?
option1: The singers of Asaph, with the vinedressers and plowmen
option2: The high priests of Aaron, with the scribes and merchants
option3: The royal archers of Benjamin, with the stonecutters and weavers
option4: The princes of Judah, with the carpenters and smiths
correct: The princes of Judah, with the carpenters and smiths
explanation: Nebuchadnezzar deported Judah's administrative elite ('princes') and skilled metalworkers and craftsmen ('carpenters and smiths') to prevent military re-armament and fortify Babylon. Jeremiah 24:1 (KJV) - " ... after that Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon had carried away captive Jeconiah the son of Jehoiakim king of Judah, and the princes of Judah, with the carpenters and smiths, from Jerusalem, and had brought them to Babylon."

question: What theological irony is exposed by the vision of the two baskets of figs in Jeremiah 24?
option1: Those who suffered the humiliation of early exile were chosen for preservation and spiritual renewal, while those who congratulated themselves on remaining in Jerusalem faced utter destruction
option2: The temple sacrifices of Jerusalem were rejected, while the offerings of the Egyptian refugees were accepted
option3: The poor plowmen were elevated to royal thrones, while the Davidic princes died in poverty
option4: The pagan Chaldeans embraced the Torah of Moses, while the priests of Zion became idolaters
correct: Those who suffered the humiliation of early exile were chosen for preservation and spiritual renewal, while those who congratulated themselves on remaining in Jerusalem faced utter destruction
explanation: Human perception was inverted: the survivors in Jerusalem assumed they were God's holy favorite remnant, but God revealed that the humiliated exiles in Babylon were the true seed of the future. Jeremiah 24:5, 8 (KJV) - "Like these good figs, so will I acknowledge them that are carried away captive ... And as the evil figs, which cannot be eaten ... So will I give Zedekiah the king of Judah, and his princes, and the residue of Jerusalem ... "

question: In which pivotal historical year - marking the battle of Carchemish - did Jeremiah deliver the definitive seventy-year prophecy in Jeremiah 25:1?
option1: The fourth year of Jehoiakim king of Judah, that was the first year of Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon
option2: The eleventh year of Zedekiah king of Judah, when the walls of Jerusalem were broken down
option3: The fourteenth year of King Hezekiah, when Sennacherib besieged the fenced cities
option4: The eighth year of King Jehoiachin, when the temple treasures were carried into exile
correct: The fourth year of Jehoiakim king of Judah, that was the first year of Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon
explanation: Dating to 605 BC, the fourth year of Jehoiakim aligned with Nebuchadnezzar's accession year after his decisive victory over Pharaoh Necho at Carchemish. Jeremiah 25:1 (KJV) - "The word that came to Jeremiah concerning all the people of Judah in the fourth year of Jehoiakim the son of Josiah king of Judah, that was the first year of Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon;"

question: How many consecutive years had Jeremiah tirelessly prophesied to Judah by the time of Chapter 25 in Jeremiah 25:3?
option1: Twelve years
option2: Three and twenty years
option3: Forty years
option4: Seventeen years
correct: Three and twenty years
explanation: From the thirteenth year of Josiah (627 BC) to the fourth year of Jehoiakim (605 BC), Jeremiah had ministered unheeded for 23 straight years. Jeremiah 25:3 (KJV) - "From the thirteenth year of Josiah the son of Amon king of Judah, even unto this day, that is the three and twentieth year, the word of the LORD hath come unto me, and I have spoken unto you, rising early and speaking; but ye have not hearkened."

question: What title of divine instrumentality does God bestow upon the pagan Babylonian emperor in Jeremiah 25:9?
option1: The rod of mine indignation and the staff of my fury
option2: The anointed shepherd of the nations from the north
option3: Nebuchadrezzar the king of Babylon, my servant
option4: The hammer of the whole earth to break the kingdoms
correct: Nebuchadrezzar the king of Babylon, my servant
explanation: God refers to the pagan conqueror Nebuchadnezzar as 'my servant' (avdi), underscoring that imperial conquerors are unwitting instruments of sovereign divine judgment. Jeremiah 25:9 (KJV) - "Behold, I will send and take all the families of the north, saith the LORD, and Nebuchadrezzar the king of Babylon, my servant, and will bring them against this land, and against the inhabitants thereof, and against all these nations round about, and will utterly destroy them, and make them an astonishment, and an hissing, and perpetual desolations."

question: What precise duration of Babylonian subjugation is prophesied for Judah and surrounding nations in Jeremiah 25:11-12?
option1: Forty years
option2: Fifty years
option3: One hundred and twenty years
option4: Seventy years
correct: Seventy years
explanation: The Babylonian exile and imperial hegemony were strictly capped by divine decree at seventy years (spanning from 605 BC to Cyrus's decree in 536 BC). Jeremiah 25:11-12 (KJV) - "And this whole land shall be a desolation, and an astonishment; and these nations shall serve the king of Babylon seventy years. And it shall come to pass, when seventy years are accomplished, that I will punish the king of Babylon, and that nation, saith the LORD, for their iniquity, and the land of the Chaldeans, and will make it perpetual desolations."

question: What symbolic vessel of divine wrath was Jeremiah commissioned to administer to all nations in Jeremiah 25:15?
option1: The wine cup of this fury
option2: The golden flagon of indignation
option3: The iron vial of the curse
option4: The silver bowl of trembling
correct: The wine cup of this fury
explanation: Jeremiah received the intoxicating chalice of divine judicial fury ('wine cup of this fury' / kos hayayin hachemah), making all surrounding nations drink to stagger into ruin. Jeremiah 25:15 (KJV) - "For thus saith the LORD God of Israel unto me; Take the wine cup of this fury at my hand, and cause all the nations, to whom I send thee, to drink it."

question: Which nation or city was first in line to drink this cup of wrath according to Jeremiah 25:18?
option1: Pharaoh king of Egypt, his servants, and all his people
option2: Jerusalem, and the cities of Judah, and the kings thereof, and the princes thereof
option3: The king of Babylon and the land of the Chaldeans
option4: Edom, Moab, and the children of Ammon
correct: Jerusalem, and the cities of Judah, and the kings thereof, and the princes thereof
explanation: Judgment begins with the household of God: Jerusalem and Judah must drink first before the cup is passed to Gentile nations. Jeremiah 25:18 (KJV) - "To wit, Jerusalem, and the cities of Judah, and the kings thereof, and the princes thereof, to make them a desolation, an astonishment, an hissing, and a curse; as it is this day;"

question: What encrypted Atbash cipher name represents the king of Babylon, who must drink the cup of wrath last of all in Jeremiah 25:26?
option1: The king of Merathaim
option2: The king of Pekod
option3: The king of Sheshach
option4: The king of Belshazzar
correct: The king of Sheshach
explanation: 'Sheshach' is an ancient Hebrew Atbash cipher (reversing alphabet letters: Tav=Aleph, Shin=Bet, Caph=Lamed) for Babel (Babylon); the ultimate imperial oppressor will drink divine vengeance last. Jeremiah 25:26 (KJV) - " ... and all the kingdoms of the world, which are upon the face of the earth: and the king of Sheshach shall drink after them."

question: What principle of divine impartiality does God announce when nations refuse to drink the cup of fury in Jeremiah 25:29?
option1: Shall the uncircumcised escape while the children of the covenant are judged in righteousness?
option2: If the righteous scarcely be saved, where shall the ungodly and the sinner appear?
option3: Behold, my hand is stretched out over all nations, and who shall turn it back?
option4: For, lo, I begin to bring evil on the city which is called by my name, and should ye be utterly unpunished? Ye shall not be unpunished: for I will call for a sword upon all the inhabitants of the earth
correct: For, lo, I begin to bring evil on the city which is called by my name, and should ye be utterly unpunished? Ye shall not be unpunished: for I will call for a sword upon all the inhabitants of the earth
explanation: If God did not spare His own chosen covenant city bearing His holy name, pagan empires have no hope of escaping His universal judicial sword. Jeremiah 25:29 (KJV) - "For, lo, I begin to bring evil on the city which is called by my name, and should ye be utterly unpunished? Ye shall not be unpunished: for I will call for a sword upon all the inhabitants of the earth, saith the LORD of hosts."

question: What loud shouting metaphor depicts Yahweh roaring against all the inhabitants of the earth in Jeremiah 25:30?
option1: He shall mightily roar upon his habitation; he shall give a shout, as they that tread the grapes, against all the inhabitants of the earth
option2: He shall sound the silver trumpet from Mount Zion like a warrior charging into battle
option3: He shall thunder with a terrible voice from the clouds like the noise of great waters
option4: He shall cry aloud from the temple of Solomon like a watchman blowing the horn
correct: He shall mightily roar upon his habitation; he shall give a shout, as they that tread the grapes, against all the inhabitants of the earth
explanation: God's roar from on high resembles the rhythmic, deafening shout (hedad) of vineyard workers stomping grapes in a winepress. Jeremiah 25:30 (KJV) - "Therefore prophesy thou against them all these words, and say unto them, The LORD shall roar from on high, and utter his voice from his holy habitation; he shall mightily roar upon his habitation; he shall give a shout, as they that tread the grapes, against all the inhabitants of the earth."

question: To what fragile falling object are the principal leaders of the flock compared when divine destruction strikes their pastures in Jeremiah 25:34?
option1: Ye shall be crushed like a bruised reed
option2: Ye shall fall like a pleasant vessel
option3: Ye shall shatter like brittle ice
option4: Ye shall perish like withered leaves
correct: Ye shall fall like a pleasant vessel
explanation: Corrupt rulers and nobles will plummet and shatter irrevocably, like an exquisite, fragile ornamental vase ('pleasant vessel' / keli chemdah) dropped onto stone. Jeremiah 25:34 (KJV) - "Howl, ye shepherds, and cry; and wallow yourselves in the ashes, ye principal of the flock: for the days of your slaughter and of your dispersions are accomplished; and ye shall fall like a pleasant vessel."

question: What strict divine injunction was given to Jeremiah regarding the integrity of his Temple Sermon proclamation in Jeremiah 26:2?
option1: Add nothing of thine own counsel
option2: Diminish not a word
option3: Speak only in the ears of the princes
option4: Seal up the scroll until the evening
correct: Diminish not a word
explanation: God prohibited theological dilution or diplomatic softening: Jeremiah was commanded to speak all divine words without omitting or editing a single syllable. Jeremiah 26:2 (KJV) - "Thus saith the LORD; Stand in the court of the LORD's house, and speak unto all the cities of Judah, which come to worship in the LORD's house, all the words that I command thee to speak unto them; diminish not a word:"

question: What infuriating historical comparison triggered a violent mob of priests, prophets, and people to seize Jeremiah in Jeremiah 26:6-9?
option1: Then will I burn this temple like the high places of Samaria
option2: Then will I deliver the Ark of the Covenant into the hands of the Philistines of Ashdod
option3: Then will I make this house like Shiloh, and will make this city a curse to all the nations of the earth
